title: BUG: GroupBy.agg with as_index=False and MultiIndex column grouping key raises ValueError
body:
## Automated contributions disclosure

I used an automated tool to develop this pull request.

- **Tool / harness:** `opencode` (open-source coding agent CLI), running under Claude Code.
- **Model:** `big-pickle` (model ID `opencode/big-pickle`).
- **Reasoning-effort / thinking setting:** this tool and model do not expose a user-selectable effort or thinking setting, so none applies. OpenCode does not publish a separate dated snapshot for this model, so the model ID above is the most specific identifier available.
- **How I used it, and what it produced:**
  - Explored the `as_index=False` + `MultiIndex`-columns code path and located the failing `_insert_inaxis_grouper` branch.
  - Drafted the change to `full_key()` and the membership check in `pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py`.
  - Wrote the two new tests in `pandas/tests/groupby/`.
  - Ran the test suites and the `ruff` checks recorded under **Verification** below.
  - Wrote the initial draft of this description, which I then reviewed, corrected, and rewrote in my own words.
  - Everything reproduced above was re-derived by me: I ran the reproduction script, confirmed the pre-fix `ValueError` and the post-fix output, reviewed every changed line, and confirmed the behaviour matches the canonical `as_index=True` + `reset_index()` form.

I reviewed and understand every change in this PR, and the commit messages are my own. I can explain the reasoning for each change on request.

---
Closes GH-39103

---

### Reproduction

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({("col0", "l0"): [0, 0, 1], ("col1", "l1"): [10, 20, 30]})
df.groupby(("col0", "l0"), as_index=False).agg({("col1", "l1"): ["min", "max"]})
```

```text
ValueError: Item must have length equal to number of levels.
```

### Root cause

`_insert_inaxis_grouper` in `pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py` decides whether the `as_index=False` group key has already been inserted by the aggregation itself. For a `MultiIndex` columns frame, the str-name path pads the key to the columns' `nlevels` (`("key", "", ...)`, per GH-17024 / GH-28549), but a tuple name of fewer levels than `result.columns.nlevels` was returned unchanged, and `result.insert(0, name, lev)` then failed with the "Item must have length equal to number of levels" `ValueError`.

### Fix

`full_key()` now also pads tuple names when `len(name) < result.columns.nlevels`, and the membership check uses `full_key(name)` so it looks up the exact key that will be inserted (previously a partial-tuple lookup which additionally raised `PerformanceWarning` on un-lex-sorted `MultiIndex` columns, surfaced as an error under CI's `filterwarnings`).

The inserted grouper column now exactly matches the canonical `groupby(..., as_index=True).agg(...).reset_index()` output.

### Verification

- Issue repro now returns the expected padded columns `[("col0", "l0", ""), ("col1", "l1", "min"), ("col1", "l1", "max")]`, byte-identical to the `as_index=True` + `reset_index()` form for `agg`, `describe`, and multi-tuple-grouper cases
- New tests: `test_groupby_agg_as_index_false_multiindex_column` (padded columns, existing column order, empty input) and `test_groupby_as_index_false_multiindex_column_matches_reset_index` (agg/describe/multi-tuple equivalence)

- Sweep of `pandas/tests/resample/`, `pandas/tests/apply/`, `pandas/tests/reshape/`: green (2 unrelated pre-existing tzdata DST failures, confirmed identical on `main`)

title: BUG: raise TypeError, not NotImplementedError, for unsupported DataFrameGroupBy transforms
body:
xref #66626, follow-up to #69717

`DataFrameGroupBy.cumsum`, `cumprod`, `cummin`, `cummax` and `rank` raised `NotImplementedError` on columns that don't support them, while the same calls on `SeriesGroupBy` raise `TypeError`:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": [0, 0, 1], "v": pd.array([b"a", b"b", b"c"], dtype="binary[pyarrow]")})
df.groupby("k")["v"].cummin()  # TypeError: cummin is not supported for binary[pyarrow] dtype
df.groupby("k").cummin()       # NotImplementedError (no message)
```

For Arrow date, time, binary, decimal and nested columns the error had no message. For object and str columns it read `function is not implemented for this dtype: [how->cummin,dtype->object]`. `DataFrameGroupBy._cython_transform` now converts the error to the same `TypeError` as `SeriesGroupBy._cython_transform`.

Tests in `test_raises.py` and `test_numeric_only.py` that accepted either exception now expect `TypeError`.

### Description

Sorting a DataFrame containing columns with PyArrow `null` type (e.g. `df.sort_values(list(df.columns))`) raised `ValueError: Categorical categories cannot be null`.

#### Root Cause
When sorting multiple columns, `DataFrame.sort_values` uses `lexsort_indexer`, which factorizes columns via `factorize(use_na_sentinel=True)` and creates `Categorical` from the resulting codes and categories. For `pa.null()`, `pa.chunked_array.dictionary_encode(null_encoding="mask")` produces a dictionary of null type containing a null element (`[<NA>]`). Because `use_na_sentinel=True` was passed, returning null categories violated the `CategoricalDtype` invariant that categories cannot contain nulls. This also caused `pd.Categorical(s)` and `s.astype("category")` to fail on `null[pyarrow]` Series.

#### Fix
In `ArrowExtensionArray.factorize`, handle `pa.types.is_null(data.type)`:
- When `use_na_sentinel=True` or array is empty: return sentinel indices (`-1`) and an empty chunked array with `pa.null()` as `uniques`.
- When `use_na_sentinel=False`: return `0` indices and `uniques` containing a single null scalar `[None]` with `pa.null()`.

#### AI Disclosure
Drafted with Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash (High), following `AGENTS.md`. The workflow reproduced the issue, implemented the fix in `ArrowExtensionArray.factorize`, added regression and unit tests in `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py`, added a release note in `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst`, verified code formatting with ruff, and verified that all existing and new test suites pass.

title: BUG: clip with missing datetime/timedelta threshold raises TypeError
body:
Closes #44785

`Series.clip` / `DataFrame.clip` with a datetime or timedelta threshold
that contains missing values raises:

```
TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'
```

because GH#40420 fills the missing thresholds with `±np.inf` before
comparing, and `±np.inf` cannot be compared against Timestamp or
timedelta values.

This change treats the missing positions explicitly: for datetime-like
thresholds the missing positions are tracked with a mask and the
original values are kept there (matching the documented behavior that
"a missing threshold will not clip the value"), while numeric
thresholds keep the existing `±np.inf` fill path untouched.

- Series threshold (lower/upper bound)
- DataFrame with a Series threshold along `axis=0` (rows) or `axis=1`
  (columns)
- DataFrame with a datetime-like DataFrame threshold

Regression tests added in `test_clip.py` for both Series and
DataFrame, plus a whatsnew entry.

<details>
<summary>Copy-pasteable example from the issue</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([1.0, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]").clip(
    pd.Series([None, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]")
)
```
</details>

cc @ghost (who diagnosed the root cause in #44785)

---

title: BLD: fix wrong banned-api comment for numpy.random
body:
- [x] closes #67994

The commented-out `"numpy.random"` banned-api entry was preceded by a note claiming "numpy.random is banned but np.random is not. Is this intentional?" — but the premise is false: TID251 resolves qualified names through aliased module imports, so with `import numpy as np` a `"numpy.random"` entry does flag `np.random.*` at the call site (verified against ruff 0.16.1).

This replaces the misleading comment with an accurate one: `numpy.random` is intentionally *not* banned because seeded `default_rng()` is legitimate, and unseeded `default_rng()` in tests is already forbidden by the pre-commit pygrep hook.

Uncommenting the entry would flag ~2,225 `np.random.*` call sites across the codebase (overwhelmingly legitimate seeded `default_rng()` uses), so that option is deliberately not taken here.

No test changes — this only edits a TOML comment. `tomllib` parses the file and `ruff check` still passes.

title: BUG: fix "boolean value of NA is ambiguous" in iloc setitem with nullable Series RHS
body:
xref: #62473

### Issue and Reproducible Example

Assigning a nullable (e.g. ``Int64``) ``Series`` containing a missing value as
the right-hand side of a ``Series.iloc`` setitem raised

    TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous

when the RHS had a non-default index:

```python
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series([4, 6, 9, None, 10, 13, 15], index=[6, 1, 5, 0, 3, 2, 4], dtype="Int64")
indices = pd.Series([6, 1, 5, 0, 3, 2, 4], dtype="int64")
values = pd.Series([4, 6, 9, None, 10, 13, 15], index=[4, 1, 2, 6, 0, 5, 3], dtype="Int64")

ser.iloc[indices] = values
```

### Root Cause

In ``_coerce_to_data_and_mask`` (``pandas/core/arrays/numeric.py``), the
precision-loss check compares the positionally-coerced float value against the
original:

```python
idx = np.nanargmax(values)
if int(values[idx]) != original[idx]:
```

``values`` is positionally aligned with the input, but when the input is a
``Series`` with a non-default index, ``original[idx]`` performs a *label* lookup
and can land on a missing (NA) element even when the value at position ``idx``
is concrete. Comparing a concrete value against NA yields NA, and the ``if``
then raises "boolean value of NA is ambiguous".

### Fix

Access the original value positionally (a ``Series`` is read via ``.iloc``;
arrays and lists are already read positionally) and skip the check when the
original value is null. ``np.nanargmax`` already guarantees ``values[idx]`` is
concrete, so the positional original is not the missing element in practice; the
null guard is defensive.

### Tests

``test_setitem_iloc_rhs_series_non_default_index_with_na`` (new, in
``pandas/tests/series/indexing/test_setitem.py``) reproduces the issue and
asserts the outcome is positional: a non-default-indexed RHS yields the same
result as the equivalent default-indexed RHS.

---
This contribution was developed with the assistance of an AI coding assistant.

title: BUG: ignore ANSI escape sequences when computing repr column widths (GH#55122)
body:
closes #55122

`to_string`/`repr` counted ANSI escape sequences (e.g. terminal colors) toward column width, so one colored cell, index label, or header misaligned every other row in its column. `_TextAdjustment.len` now ignores them, and `justify` pads by display width when a column contains one — the same approach `_EastAsianTextAdjustment` already uses. `adjoin` also now sizes its last column with `strlen` rather than builtin `len`; without that, a colored Series got trailing padding. This changes two East Asian `adjoin` test expectations (padding the last column to display width, consistent with plain text), but no real repr output.

Plain-text output takes the old path after a single `"\x1b"` check per column, so DataFrame `to_string` timings are within noise; `Series.to_string` is ~7% slower (~2 ms per 20k rows) from the `adjoin` change.

Tradeoff for reviewers: output that is viewed raw (a file, or a console that doesn't interpret escapes) now aligns as rendered rather than by raw character count. Related: GH-18066 (terminal styling).

title: BUG: IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__ ignores struct validity bitmap
body:

added a test that checks both plain and chunked arrow arrays — makes sure null struct entries show up as NA correctly. all 10 existing interval pyarrow tests still pass.

title: ENH: respect display.precision for complex and float Interval values (GH#25920)
body:
closes #25920

Float sequences already follow `display.precision` (GH-60503). This extends that to:

- complex numbers in object-dtype Series/DataFrame cells, including ones nested in sequences

### Description
When passing a `Grouper` with `sort=True` inside a list (e.g. `df.groupby([pd.Grouper(key="k", sort=True)])`), `Grouper._set_grouper` physically reordered the underlying object for non-monotonic axes, but `get_grouper`'s list path discarded the reordered object. body:
- [x] closes #56454
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature

- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)
- [x] If I used AI to develop this pull request, I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`.

`a.merge(b, on="key", how="left")` and `b.merge(a, on="key", how="right")` describe the same logical join, but the shared key column's dtype depended on which frame `.merge()` was called on, not on `how`. `_get_merge_keys` always drops the shared join-key column from `self.right` and keeps it from `self.left`, regardless of `how`. `_maybe_add_join_keys` normally reconciles this via `find_common_type` when there are missing/unmatched rows to fill, but when every row already lines up 1:1 (both `left_indexer` and `right_indexer` are `None`), that reconciliation step is skipped entirely, so the output silently kept `self.left`'s dtype even for a right join.

This adds a narrowly-scoped case: only when `how == "right"` and no reindexing is needed on either side, use the right frame's original key array/dtype (mirroring how a left join already keeps the left frame's dtype in that same situation). `how="right"` merges that do need reindexing/filling are untouched and continue to go through the existing `find_common_type` reconciliation path unchanged.

One existing test (`test_merge_ea_and_non_ea`) asserted the old (buggy) behavior for `how="right"` and has been updated to reflect the corrected, symmetric dtype.

## Summary

Implements `RangeIndex.isin` directly (GH#66263). When the query `values` are smaller than the index, the new fast path allocates only the boolean result array and checks membership with O(1) `range.__contains__`, computing the target location via `(val - start) // step`. This avoids materializing the full integer array (`self._values`, e.g. an 80MB array for a 10M-entry range) that the generic `algos.isin` path allocates.

- For `len(values) < len(self)`, use the O(1) `range.__contains__` fast path.
- For `len(values) >= len(self)`, delegate to `super().isin` as before.
- Non-sized iterables (e.g. generators) are delegated to the base implementation, preserving `Index.isin` behavior.

## Tests

Added coverage in `pandas/tests/indexes/ranges/test_range.py`:
- Correctness of the fast path across positive/negative steps, negative starts, missing values, and empty queries.
- Agreement with the materialized `Index.isin` for mixed-value queries.
- The fast path does not touch `_values` (via a monkeypatched property that raises).
- Set / non-numeric / generator inputs and the `level` kwarg.
- Fallback to the generic implementation for large queries and TypeError for non-list-like values.

title: ENH: sniff sep=None with the C engine in read_csv (GH#9645)
body:
closes #9645

`read_csv(sep=None)` used to fall back to the python engine. `TextFileReader` now sniffs the separator with `csv.Sniffer` on the first row that isn't skipped, blank or a comment, then gives the C parser a small wrapper that replays the data read so far. That works for non-seekable handles too. On a 500k x 8 `;`-separated file this takes the read from 1.76s to 0.13s.

pyarrow still raises/falls back as before.

Differences from the python engine's sniffing:
- A leading blank line is skipped; the python engine raises `Could not determine delimiter`.
- A file with no row to sniff raises the C engine's `EmptyDataError` instead of `csv.Error`.
- If the sniffer picks a separator wider than one utf-8 byte (possible with quoted fields, e.g. `"a"§"b"`), this raises a `ValueError` suggesting `engine="python"`. Previously the default engine fell back to python, with a warning. Falling back from inside `_make_engine` would mean re-cleaning options for the python engine, which seemed not worth it for this case, but I'm open to it.

title: PERF: Speed up `import pandas` with PEP 810 lazy imports
body:
[PEP 810](https://peps.python.org/pep-0810/) (explicit lazy imports, CPython 3.15+) lets a module defer imports via a `__lazy_modules__` declaration. On older Pythons the attribute is simply ignored, so adding it is backward compatible. A small set of pandas subsystems are imported eagerly today but are only needed once a specific entry point is called. Deferring them with `__lazy_modules__` keeps them out of a plain `import pandas`:

- the I/O backends — `read_*` / `to_*` / Excel / parquet / html / sql / json /
  stata / sas / … and the optional third-party engines they pull in;
- `pandas.testing` (the `assert_*` helpers);
- the `eval` / `query`, `resample`, `interchange`, and `pandas.api` re-export stacks.

Make more imports lazy would require reworking `pandas.core` as the many dependencies in modules there make it hard to use PEP 810 without additional changes.

**Benchmarks**

The import time depends a bit on the workload, so adding multiple benchmarks. 

| workload (after `import pandas`) | baseline: modules / ms | lazy: modules / ms | faster |
|---|---|---|---|
| import pandas (nothing else) | 290 / 826 | 221 / 678 | 18% |
| pd.DataFrame({'a':[1,2,3],'b':[4,5,6]}) | 290 / 838 | 221 / 682 | 19% |
| df.groupby('a').sum() | 290 / 834 | 221 / 685 | 18% |
| pd.to_datetime([...]) | 290 / 836 | 221 / 704 | 16% |
| df.eval('a + b') | 290 / 843 | 229 / 715 | 15% |
| df.to_csv() | 291 / 832 | 222 / 706 | 15% |
| pd.read_csv(StringIO) | 290 / 834 | 265 / 812 | 3% |
| pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df, df) | 290 / 840 | 229 / 710 | 15% |

title: BUG: DataFrame.apply/agg with a callable dropped the extension dtype (GH#61812)
body:
closes #61812

`DataFrame.agg`/`apply` with a callable that reduces each column (or row) to a scalar built the result from the raw Python scalars, so the frame's extension dtype was lost — `df.agg(lambda x: x.mean())` on a `double[pyarrow]` frame returned `float64`, where the string alias `df.agg("mean")` returned `double[pyarrow]`. This routes those results through `ExtensionArray._cast_pointwise_result`, the mechanism `DataFrameGroupBy.agg` already uses for a callable, when the frame has a single extension dtype. Masked frames lost the dtype the same way and are fixed too.

Sparse frames are excluded: a reduction result has no sparsity to preserve, and `SparseArray`'s cast drops a timezone (GH-61812 does not fix that; it is reachable today through `groupby.agg`). `category` frames are excluded too, since the result dtype would depend on whether the values are categories.

`DataFrame.nunique` and `DataFrame.corrwith` are implemented via `self.apply`, so each casts its result back to what it returned before — `nunique` to `int64` (matching `count()` and `groupby.nunique`) and `corrwith` to `float64` (a correlation coefficient would otherwise come back as `Int64` for an all-NA result). Neither method changes behavior.

Not covered here: `df.agg([f])` and `df.agg({"col": f})` assemble results through a different path and still drop the dtype, as they already do on main relative to `df.agg(["mean"])`.

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray ops leak pyarrow errors for unconvertible operands (GH#62682)
body:
closes #62682

`ArrowExtensionArray` binary ops let pyarrow's own `ArrowInvalid`/`ArrowTypeError` escape when the
other operand holds objects pyarrow cannot convert — `Categorical`, `Interval`, `DateOffset`, a bare
`object()`. Arithmetic and logical ops now raise pandas' own `TypeError`; comparisons compare
elementwise for `==`/`!=` and raise `TypeError` for ordered comparisons, matching the NumPy-nullable
dtypes.

Note that the issue's *literal* repro already gives a clean `TypeError` on `main` — `pd.array(["a", np.nan])`
is the arrow-backed `str` dtype, which GH-65677 routed through an object-dtype fallback. The bug is
live for every other arrow dtype:

```python
pd.array([1, 2], dtype="int64[pyarrow]") + pd.DataFrame([[pd.Categorical(["test"])] * 2])
# main:    pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: ... did not recognize Python value type
# this PR: TypeError: operation 'add' not supported for dtype 'int64[pyarrow]' with dtype 'object'
```

This also fixes `duration[ns][pyarrow] == Hour(1)`, which raised `ArrowTypeError` while the reflected
`Hour(1) == arr` worked. `!=` against an offset scalar needs the reflected-`__ne__` detour:
`BaseOffset.__ne__` is `not self == other`, which raises on an array result, so `ne` is evaluated as
a negated `eq`.

The 2-D-ndarray guard and the comparison length-mismatch `ValueError` from the same issue landed
separately in GH-68458; this PR is rebased on top of it.

title: BUG: concat and shift with an ExtensionDtype IntervalDtype subtype (GH#64297)
body:
closes #64297

Two fixes for an `IntervalDtype` with an extension dtype subtype:

* `IntervalArray._concat_same_type` used `np.concatenate`, which downgraded a masked subtype to its NumPy counterpart (`interval[Int64]` -> `interval[int64]`) and boxed tz-aware endpoints to object. A non-empty result was re-inferred back, but an empty one has nothing to infer from, so `pd.concat([pd.Series(empty_tz_interval)])` raised `TypeError: category, object, and string subtypes are not supported`. `concat_compat` fixes both, and `Index.append` with it. This is also why a non-empty `Int64` read through `IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` came back as `interval[float64]`.
* `IntervalArray.shift` built its NA fill piece with `from_breaks([na_scalar] * (n + 1))`, which infers `datetime64[s]`. Once the endpoints are concatenated dtype-faithfully that stops being a loud failure and becomes a silently wrong one: `Series(interval[timedelta64[us]]).shift(1)` returned `interval[datetime64[s]]`. Building the fill piece with `take(..., allow_fill=True)` keeps the subtype, and also stops `float32` being upcast to `float64`.

GH-67897 has since made `IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` delegate to an extension subtype's own `__from_arrow__`. The only part of this PR left there is the empty-input case, which still raised `TypeError: Cannot interpret 'Int64Dtype()' as a data type` for a masked subtype.

Two related things deliberately left out of scope, both filed:

* The write side, GH-67753. `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes its arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype` and so rejects every extension subtype, which is why the tz-aware array in GH-64297 has to be built by hand. Lifting that alone would produce unreadable parquet: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Making that round-trip needs a metadata-format change on a registered extension type.
* `__from_arrow__` ignores the struct-level validity bitmap, GH-67754, so a null struct entry whose children are non-null reads back as `(0.0, 0.0]` instead of NaN. Pre-existing, and not reachable from pandas-written data since `__arrow_array__` nulls the children too.

title: BUG: concat(union_categories=True) conflated True with 1
body:
`concat(union_categories=True)` silently replaced `True` with `1` when unioning bool-category and integer-category Categoricals:

```python
a = Series(Categorical([1, 2, 3]))
b = Series(Categorical([True, False]))

concat([a, b], ignore_index=True, union_categories=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, 1, False]     <- True became 1
concat([a, b], ignore_index=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, True, False]  <- the default gets it right
```

`union_categories_compat` casts categories with differing dtypes to a common dtype, which for bool and integer categories is object. `union_categoricals` then unions the categories through a hashtable, where `True` and `1` collide, so one replaces the other. The existing `is_unique` guard only caught collapse within a single input, not across inputs.

A Categorical's categories must be unique and uniqueness is decided by hash, so no Categorical can hold both `1` and `True` and there is nothing to return here. `union_categories_compat` now returns `None` when the categories cannot be shown to be all distinct, and the caller casts to object before continuing — returning `None` is not enough on its own, because two object-dtype `CategoricalDtype`s compare equal whenever their categories do, so `dtypes_all_equal` would send the inputs straight back into `union_categoricals`. The result is object dtype with both values intact.

The check is a single pass keyed by the category itself: it refuses a key that turns up under two different kinds. Plain numbers, Python or NumPy, are one kind, so `1`/`1.0` merge as they do for int64 and float64 categories; every other type is its own kind, so `True`/`1`, an `IntEnum` or `StrEnum` member and its value, and `Decimal("1")`/`1` are refused. Duplicate column labels still read back as duplicate columns, and the check also refuses a pair whose comparison raises rather than letting the error out of `concat` (`Decimal("1")` and `np.int64(1)` hash equal and raise on `==`). Inputs that share one categories object are scanned once, since a categories Index cannot collide with itself. An `inferred_type` shortcut was tried and dropped — an `IntEnum` infers as `"integer"` just as `int` does, so it could not see that case.

Follow-up to GH-65098, which added the `union_categories` keyword in the unreleased 3.1.0 — no whatsnew entry for that reason.

title: BUG: DataFrame repr ignores display.width when max_columns=0 (GH#21337)
body:
closes #21337

With `display.max_columns=0` (the default in a terminal), the DataFrame repr fit its columns to `shutil.get_terminal_size()` and ignored an explicitly set `display.width`, so both `width=10000` (don't truncate) and `width=40` (truncate harder) had no effect.

Just using `display.width` there would cap every default terminal repr at 80, since the default of 80 is indistinguishable from a user-set 80. So this changes the `display.width` default to `None`, matching its documented "set to None to auto-detect" meaning: interactive terminals still auto-detect their width, an explicit int is now honored, and scripts fall back to the terminal size (80 when stdout is not a tty), so their output is unchanged. The notebook/qtconsole fallback stays at 80.

This is a repost of GH-66004, which was closed for lack of review rather than rejected.

title: BUG: DataFrame.clip with an extension-dtype array/Index bound degrades to object
body:
`NDFrame._clip_with_one_bound` converts a non-`Series` list-like bound via `_align_for_op(threshold, axis, flex=None)` and passes the result to `where`. Since GH-61828 that routes an extension-dtype operand through `_maybe_align_series_as_frame`, which now returns an EA-columned `DataFrame` instead of the `Series` it used to return. `DataFrame.where` has an EA-aware column-wise path for a 1-D `other` but none for a 2-D one, so the bound interleaves to an object ndarray.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 20], [30, 40]])

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1).dtypes
# object, object   (int64, int64 before GH-61828)

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1, inplace=True)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[[15]]' for dtype 'int64'
```

`_align_for_op` now skips that broadcast when `flex is None` — clip is that flag's only caller — so the bound stays a `Series` and takes the working 1-D path; the helper is renamed `_align_series_as_frame` since it no longer has a fallback. `_clip_with_one_bound` then pins `axis=1` when it gets a `Series` back with `axis=None`, since `_align_for_op` had already aligned the bound against `self.columns` and `DataFrame.align(Series, axis=None)` raises.

The object degradation never shipped, so against released 3.0 the only `clip` change is that `df.clip(lower=<extension-dtype array>)` with `axis` omitted no longer raises `ValueError: Must specify axis=0 or 1`.

Routing the bound back through the 1-D path made it reach `np_can_hold_element`'s `dtype.itemsize < tipo.itemsize` comparison, which runs before the `not isinstance(tipo, np.dtype)` guard and so raised `AttributeError` for any non-NumPy `tipo` carrying no `itemsize`. That is a released bug in its own right, not just a `clip` one: on 3.0 it fires for every setitem-shaped path that hands a `SparseArray` into an integer-dtype NumPy column.

```python
ser = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
sp = pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 2, 3])

ser.where([True, False, True], sp)                              # AttributeError on 3.0
ser.mask([True, False, True], sp)                               # AttributeError on 3.0
ser[[0, 1]] = sp[:2]                                            # AttributeError on 3.0
pd.Index([10, 20, 30]).putmask(np.array([True, False, True]), sp)  # AttributeError on 3.0
```

The comparison is now skipped when the dtype carries no `itemsize`; such an element falls through to the extension-array branch below, which re-runs the same guards on its values densified with the sparse subtype (as in GH-68457), so a `SparseArray` is accepted or rejected as the nullable spelling is.

title: BUG: DataFrame.agg with a list of funcs rounds uint64 results (GH#65031)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65031, which added the list-of-reductions fast path in
`FrameApply._agg_list_like_frame_reductions`. That path computes DataFrame-level reductions per
dtype group and stacks one 1-row frame per function with `concat`. When the functions return
signed and unsigned integers, the common dtype of the stack is float64, which rounds values
above 2**53:

```python
big = 2**64 - 3
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Series([big, 1], dtype="uint64")})

df.agg(["max", "count"])
# main:   max -> 1.8446744073709552e+19, dtype float64   (true value 18446744073709551613)
# 3.0.6:  max -> 18446744073709551613,   dtype object
```

The `uint64[pyarrow]` spelling raised `ArrowInvalid` on the same cast instead of rounding.

Now, when a dtype group's results mix a signed with an unsigned integer (numpy, masked, arrow or
sparse) and their common dtype is a float, that group is stacked as object. The rule looks only
at dtypes, so the result dtype does not depend on the values, and the lossy cast is never
attempted. This matches 3.0.6 for numpy, masked and sparse `uint64`. Every other group keeps
the common-dtype stacking, so e.g. `int64` with `["sum", "mean"]` stays float64 (as in 3.0 and
`Series.agg`), including sums above 2**53.

No whatsnew: the rounding came in with the unreleased GH-65031 fast path.

title: REF: remove Series._constructor_expanddim_from_mgr (GH#56681)
body:
Human: closes #56681, as everything remaining has downstream packages that rely on overriding them, so it would be more effort than its worth to further simplify.

---

GH-56681 lists a pile of `_constructor*` / `*_from_mgr` methods that could plausibly be trimmed. This removes one of them.

`Series.to_frame` was the only caller of `_constructor_expanddim_from_mgr`. It now builds the DataFrame with `DataFrame._from_mgr` and, for subclasses, hands that to `_constructor_expanddim` -- which is exactly what the removed method did.

Subclasses give up nothing measurable. Benchmarking a subclass that overrides the hook against one relying on `_constructor_expanddim`: 35.6us vs 36.2us, i.e. inside the noise, because `to_2d_mgr` dominates `to_frame`.

That is *not* true of the sibling `_constructor_sliced_from_mgr`, so I am leaving that one alone: the equivalent removal costs a geopandas-shaped subclass 3.3x on `gdf["geometry"]` (5.5us -> 18.3us) and 2.3x on `.iloc[0]`, since the fallback pays for a second `Series.__init__`.

A downstream override left in place is simply no longer called. Of the libraries that define it -- geopandas and timely-beliefs -- both have a `_constructor_expanddim` that produces the same result, just via their own constructor. Same treatment `_sliced_from_mgr` and `_expanddim_from_mgr` got in GH-57553.

title: BUG: inaccurate Series.corr for nearly-constant data (GH#59652)
body:
closes #59652

The out-of-range `DataFrame.corr` result reported in the issue was already clamped by GH-61154, and -1 is the exact answer there. But `Series.corr` on the same data still returned -0.707. Its helper centers once, and when the values differ by ~1 ulp the rounding error in the mean dominates.

`nanops._pearson_corr` now uses the corrected two-pass formula (subtracts the leftover mean from the dot products), so it returns -1.0. It also fixes constant data whose mean rounds inexactly, e.g. `Series([0.1] * 3).corr(Series([0., 1, 2]))`, which returned 0.0 instead of NaN.

To keep this from costing speed, the arrays are only rescaled when their magnitude is outside 1e±50 (where the product of the sums of squares could overflow/underflow), and the max-abs uses `max(a.max(), -a.min())` to avoid a temporary. Net, the helper is ~15-22% faster than main at n=100 / 10k / 1M. Against main's version, results agree within 7e-16 on 2000 random cases across magnitudes 1e±200 and on inf / subnormal / float32 / bool edge cases, apart from the two intended changes.

`DataFrame.corrwith(method="pearson")` has a separate vectorized formula with the same single-centering issue; left for a follow-up.

title: BUG: Timedelta/Timestamp overflow guards broke on ndarray subclasses (GH#66552)
body:
Follow-up to the GH-66552 overflow-guard series (#66581, #66661, #66668, #66670, #66692) and to GH-43178 (#65515), all unreleased.

Every guard those PRs added either reduces with `np.max(..., initial=/where=)` or views the operand as `i8`, and both assume an exact `np.ndarray`:

```python
pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.ma.array([2.0, 3.0])
# TypeError: MaskedArray.max() got an unexpected keyword argument 'initial'
#   (initial= makes numpy dispatch to the subclass's own max(); np.matrix too)

pd.Timedelta(5, "ns") + np.ma.MaskedArray(np.array([10, 20], "M8[ns]"), mask=[False, True])
# array(['...015', '...025'], dtype='datetime64[ns]')   <- mask silently dropped,
#   masked payload exposed as a real timestamp; numpy gives masked_array([15, --])
```

Affected: `_addsub_timedelta64_array` and `_addsub_datetime64_array` in both `timedeltas.pyx` and `timestamps.pyx`, `_mul_numeric_array`, `_check_div_float_array`, and `TimedeltaArray._mul_float_overflowsafe` — the last one via `TimedeltaIndex`/`Series`, and it left the EA holding a `MaskedArray` whose `repr` raised `MaskError` even before #65515.

Each guard now measures a plain view of the operand and leaves the arithmetic itself on the subclass, so the overflow raise survives and so does the subclass. `_mul_float_overflowsafe` instead strips the subclass up front, since its result has to be a `TimedeltaArray` either way — that also makes its float branch agree with its integer branch, which already read through to the raw values.

The same `_addsub_*` helpers also read only the *base* unit out of the operand's dtype, so a multiplier was discarded:

```python
pd.Timedelta(1, "s") + np.array([1], "m8[10s]")
# array([2], dtype='timedelta64[s]')   <- every value came back divided by 10
```

`m8[10s]` is not a resolution pandas can hold, and GH-25611 (#68072) already rejects those dtypes everywhere an array of them can enter — the constructors, `pd.array`, a `dtype=` argument, and `DatetimeIndex`/`Series`/`TimedeltaIndex` arithmetic. These three helpers were the remaining hole, so they raise `ValueError` too. The whatsnew note for GH-25611 covers the added case.

`TimedeltaIndex` is otherwise unaffected throughout because it goes through `np.asarray` first.

title: BUG: replace inplace with many values used quadratic memory (GH#25816)
body:
closes #25816

With `inplace=True` and a list-like or dict `to_replace`, `Block.replace_list` materialized one full-length boolean mask per value before replacing, so peak memory was n_values * len(data) bytes (a 10**6-key dict on 10**6 rows asks for ~1TB). The masks were materialized only so they would be computed against the original values rather than the partially-replaced ones. When that list would be larger than the values themselves, this instead compares against a copy of the values and keeps the masks lazy, so memory is O(len(data)) and replacements still do not chain (`{1: 2, 2: 3}` maps 1 to 2). With only a few values (fewer than the itemsize), materializing is still cheaper and is kept, so small inplace replaces do not use more memory than before.

The non-inplace path already built masks lazily. It is still O(n_values * len(data)) in time; that is GH-6697 and is left for a separate PR.

body:

`Styler.to_latex` (and so `DataFrame.to_latex`) applied the `styler.render.max_elements` / `max_rows` / `max_columns` trimming meant for HTML display. title: BUG: retain DatetimeIndex freq in concat regardless of input order (GH#64253)
body:
- [x] closes #64253
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

### Problem

`union_indexes` combines `DatetimeIndex` inputs pairwise. When an intermediate union is not contiguous (e.g. `s1 ∪ s3` before `s2` is added), `DatetimeIndex._union` falls back to the generic set path and `_with_freq("infer")`. Inference cannot recover an offset such as `CustomBusinessDay(holidays=...)` from the values, so `freq` becomes `None` and stays `None`, making the result depend on the order of the inputs. The same path is hit by `pd.DataFrame({dict of Series})`.

The bug still reproduces on current `main`; the earlier "not replicable" comment on the issue mistook the `Pandas4Warning` about the default `sort` for the assertion failing.

### Fix

Following the review on the previous attempt (#66295): do not try to preserve `freq` at every pairwise step; validate once at the end. A private helper `_maybe_restore_freq` is called at the two points where the combined index is final (`union_indexes` "special" branch, and after `safe_sort_index` in `_get_combined_index`). It is a no-op unless the result is a monotonic `DatetimeIndex` with `freq is None` and *all* inputs are `DatetimeIndex` sharing the same non-None `freq`; in that case it runs `_validate_frequency` against the final values and re-attaches the `freq` only if they conform. Nothing is inferred, and non-conforming results (e.g. the tz-aware `America/Santiago` DST case from the issue, which has a real gap) keep `freq=None`.

### Test

`test_concat_datetimeindex_freq_order_independent` is parametrized over `sort=True/False/None` (the `None` case also asserts the existing `Pandas4Warning`). Without the fix the `True` and `None` cases fail; with it all three pass. `pandas/tests/indexes`, `frame`, `series`, `reshape`, `resample`, `tseries`, `window`, `groupby` pass locally.

title: BUG: std/sem on Arrow date columns read the result in days or ms as seconds
body:
`std()` and `sem()` on Arrow date columns returned the wrong answer.

For the dates Jan 1, Jan 3, Jan 2, Jan 6 (2020), `std()` should be about 2.16 days. pandas returned 2 seconds for `date32[pyarrow]` and 2,160 days for `date64[pyarrow]`.

Arrow stores `date32` as days since 1970 and `date64` as milliseconds since 1970. pandas computed the std of those numbers correctly, then labelled the result as seconds without converting it.

Fix:
- `date32`: convert to seconds before computing (the same path as `timestamp[s]`).
- `date64`: keep the result in milliseconds and return `duration[ms]` instead of `duration[s]`, matching what subtracting two `date64` values already returns.

Both now return `2 days 03:50:45`, the same as NumPy `datetime64`.

title: BUG: preserve NaN and NA in nullable CSV floats
body:
# BUG: preserve NaN and NA in nullable CSV floats

Closes #65237

## TL;DR

This fixes an issue where `read_csv()` could not preserve the distinction between a parser-recognized missing value (`pd.NA`) and an IEEE `NaN` value when reading into pandas nullable floating dtypes.

The final fix works across the regular CSV parsers and the PyArrow engine, while keeping the existing behavior for NumPy float dtypes, categorical data, integer dtypes, and invalid numeric strings.

I initially tried a smaller parser-only fix. After tracing the value through the full conversion path, I found a separate information-loss point in the PyArrow path. The final implementation therefore reuses pandas' existing nullable-array semantics and only adds lossless Arrow float handling when the user explicitly requests a pandas nullable floating dtype.

## What was happening

With `future.distinguish_nan_and_na=True`, pandas can represent these as two different values:

* `pd.NA`: a missing value
* `np.nan`: an actual floating-point NaN

For example:

```python
data = """,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan"""

pd.read_csv(
    StringIO(data),
    index_col=0,
    dtype={"x": "Float64"},
    keep_default_na=False,
    na_values=[""],
)
```

The expected result is:

```text
a     1.0
b    <NA>
c     NaN
dtype: Float64
```

The empty field is explicitly listed in `na_values`, so it should remain missing. The literal `"nan"` is not listed as missing, so in distinguish mode it should remain an IEEE NaN.

Before this change, the regular parser path raised while converting the `"nan"` literal.

## Regular parser path

`NumericArray._from_sequence_of_strings()` delegates numeric parsing to `to_numeric(errors="raise")`.

`to_numeric()` accepts normal numeric and infinity strings, but intentionally rejects NaN strings. Changing that globally would broaden the behavior of `to_numeric()` beyond this bug.

Instead, the nullable floating conversion path recognizes valid NaN literals and converts them to `np.nan` before calling `to_numeric()`.

After conversion, the NaN positions are restored through normal nullable-array assignment:

```python
scalars[nan_mask] = np.nan
```

This means pandas' existing nullable-array semantics decide whether the value is masked as NA or preserved as NaN, rather than duplicating that logic by manually changing `_data` or `_mask`.

This is consistent with the NaN/NA behavior established in [[#62040](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62040)](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62040).

## PyArrow path

While testing the same case across parser engines, I found a separate issue in the PyArrow path.

At the Arrow level, the distinction is still preserved:

```text
[1.0, null, NaN]
```

But converting the Arrow table through NumPy float64 collapses both values:

```text
Arrow table
    ↓
table.to_pandas()
    ↓
NumPy float64
    ↓
[1.0, NaN, NaN]
```

At that point pandas can no longer determine which NaN originally came from an Arrow null.

This is similar to the lossy intermediate-conversion problem handled in [[#62053](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62053)](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62053).

I first tried mapping all Arrow floating columns through pandas nullable floating dtypes. That fixed #65237, but also changed categorical category dtypes from NumPy `float64` to pandas `Float64`, causing parser regressions.

The final implementation is therefore narrower:

* Arrow floats are preserved through nullable `Float32` / `Float64` only when the user explicitly requests a pandas nullable floating dtype.
* Categorical, NumPy float, and unspecified columns stay on their existing conversion paths.
* Temporary nullable numeric dtypes for columns not explicitly requested by the user are converted back to their original NumPy dtype.

This preserves the information needed for #65237 without changing unrelated dtype behavior.

## NaN literal boundary check

The regular parser recognizes the canonical NaN forms:

```text
nan
+nan
-nan
```

case-insensitively and with surrounding whitespace ignored.

I checked the predicate against Python float parsing across 397 combinations covering:

* upper/lower case
* optional `+` / `-`
* spaces, tabs, and newlines
* ordinary numeric values
* infinity values
* malformed tokens

There were no mismatches for NaN recognition.

Other numeric parsing remains delegated to `to_numeric()`.

## Validation

Regression test for #65237:

```text
8 passed
```

This covers all parser variants and both NaN/NA modes.

Categorical parser tests after narrowing the PyArrow mapping:

```text
315 passed
9 xfailed
0 failed
```

Full non-network parser suite:

```text
6128 passed
186 skipped
60 deselected
124 xfailed
0 failed
```

Additional nullable numeric/parser coverage:

```text
1977 passed
8 skipped
15 xfailed
0 failed
```

Code checks:

```text
pre-commit: passed
git diff --check: passed
```

## Related

* Issue: [[#65237](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65237)](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65237)
* NaN/NA nullable-array semantics: [[#62040](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62040)]
* Related Arrow lossless conversion work: [[#62053](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62053)]
* Related Float64/NaN write-path fix: [[#65038](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65038)]
* Related NaN/NA regression coverage: [[#64854](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64854)]

## Note

I found this issue particularly interesting because the visible bug was in `read_csv()`, but the actual behavior crossed several layers: parser token handling, nullable arrays, NumPy representation, and Arrow-to-pandas conversion.

The first working patch was much smaller, but tracing the value through those layers exposed a second information-loss point in the PyArrow path. That made this a useful example of why even a relatively small data bug can benefit from following the representation end-to-end before deciding where the fix should live.

I had not looked this closely before at how pandas distinguishes missing values from IEEE NaN internally, so this was also a useful way to understand that part of the stack while contributing a concrete fix.

Dedicated to Moe Jia.

title: Fix/parallel read csv converters
body:
Closes #68505

### Summary

Keep user-defined `converters` eligible for parallel `read_csv`, but turn thread-affinity failures from converter worker threads into an actionable error.

Most converters are safe to run in parser workers. A converter that captures a thread-affine resource, such as a SQLite connection created on the caller thread, cannot safely use that resource from a worker thread.

Fixes two off-by-a-dimension bugs in `ExponentialMovingWindow.online` that cause it to ignore the decay for single-column DataFrames, returning the unweighted cumulative mean instead of the exponentially weighted mean.

Regression coverage added for single-column DataFrames (both the initial and `update` paths).

title: BUG: Rolling/Expanding skew and kurt wrong on data with a large shared offset
body:
The sliding moment accumulators behind `Rolling.skew`/`kurt` (and `Expanding.skew`/`kurt`, which
share the kernels) take every deviation against a running mean. On a series carrying a large
offset the mean dwarfs the spread, so the deviations lose most of their significant digits and the
results are silently wrong — on a 4-wide window of values one ulp apart at 1e8, `kurt` returned
213, where the attainable range for 4 points is [-6, 4]. Separately, once a window held values spanning nearly the
whole `float64` range, every later window returned `NaN`.

This anchors the accumulators to each window's first value so an offset shared by the window
cancels exactly, retires that anchor once the window's centre drifts away from it, and replaces
the per-kernel cancellation tests with a shared detector (checking for NaN, anchor drift, and
peak deviation). It is the treatment `Rolling.cov`/`corr` already received in GH-66678.

The NaN-forever half is a long-standing bug (the empty-window variant was fixed separately in
GH-69123); the low-variance half surfaced in GH-64366, which
dropped the `m2 <= nobs * 1e-14` guard that had been returning `NaN` there instead of a wrong
number. The underlying precision loss predates both — 2.3.3 pre-centred the values by the rounded
global mean, and GH-62863/GH-63143 dropped that when they introduced the incremental instability
machinery.

Dropping the two per-kernel arms also removes the rescan-every-window fallbacks they triggered, so
this is a speedup as well as an accuracy fix:
`pd.Series(np.tile([-1., 0., 1., 0.], 25_000)).expanding().skew()` goes from 5.3s to 0.7ms (the
old behaviour was quadratic in the length of the series), and
`pd.Series(rng.lognormal(0, 5, 50_000)).rolling(1000).kurt()` from 54ms to 0.6ms.

Accuracy, measured against an exact rational oracle over 83,772 windows per statistic (142 series
× 6 window widths, covering shared offsets, drifting levels, lognormal, mixed-magnitude and
NaN-holed data):

| | p99 rel err | max rel err |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` before | 3.3e+01 | 4.6e+23 |
| `skew` after | 1.0e-11 | 4.9e-08 |
| `kurt` before | 4.8e+02 | 2.9e+32 |
| `kurt` after | 1.8e-10 | 3.5e-07 |

No window in that sweep comes back worse than `main` by more than 1e-6 relative.

Two consequences worth calling out. A window of identical values reached incrementally on offset
data used to come back as a number rather than `NaN`, because the digits the accumulators had lost
left `m2` nonzero; it is `NaN` now, which is what GH-62864 already specifies for a degenerate
window. And the new detector is not free on data that never needed it: in an ABBA-ordered
measurement with untouched `rolling.median`/`var` as controls, `rolling(100).skew()` is 2.6% slower
on uniform data and 12.5% slower on lognormal data, against the wins above.

One known limit, pre-existing and deliberately not widened into here: the same
overflow-in-the-detector shape affects `roll_var` and the `cov`/`corr` diagonal.

title: BUG: read_parquet/to_parquet fall back to fsspec when pyarrow can't build the filesystem (GH#58078)
body:
closes #58078

With the pyarrow engine and no `storage_options`, `_get_path_or_handle` first tries `pyarrow.fs.FileSystem.from_uri` and falls back to fsspec only on `TypeError`/`ArrowInvalid`. For `hdfs:///path` (empty host, meaning "use `fs.defaultFS` from core-site.xml"), Arrow builds the namenode as `"hdfs://"` and libhdfs raises `OSError`, so the call fails instead of falling back. fsspec's `HadoopFileSystem` handles this URL (it defaults to `host="default"`), which is why the reporter's `storage_options={}` workaround works.

An `OSError` now falls back too, but only for `hdfs:///` URLs (no host): otherwise it is a real error (e.g. `OSError: Bucket '...' not found` from S3), and falling back would replace it with a misleading fsspec/s3fs `ImportError`. If the fsspec fallback also fails, pyarrow's error is chained as its cause. Separately, `ArrowInvalid` is widened to `ArrowException` so that `ArrowNotImplementedError` (pyarrow built without a given filesystem) falls back too. The test registers an in-memory fsspec implementation for `hdfs` and round-trips `hdfs:///...`; pyarrow raises `OSError` there whether or not libhdfs is installed. Other tests check that an `OSError` propagates for other schemes and for `hdfs://` with a host, and that pyarrow's error is chained when fsspec also fails.

title: BUG: raise instead of silently falling back in array strftime (GH#58178)
body:
closes #58178

`DatetimeArray.strftime` (and so `DatetimeIndex.strftime`, `Series.dt.strftime`, and `to_csv(date_format=...)`) caught any `ValueError` from `Timestamp.strftime` and quietly substituted `str(ts)`, giving e.g. `['1820-01-01 00:00:00', '20']` for `%y`. This takes the issue's "always raise" alternative rather than adding an `errors=` keyword. The error now propagates, matching `Timestamp.strftime` and `PeriodArray.strftime` (which already raises `Invalid format string`, GH-53562).

On POSIX, `datetime.strftime` essentially never raises `ValueError`, so this only changes behavior on Windows (`%y` before 1900 on Python < 3.14, directives MSVC doesn't support such as `%-d`). The new test is therefore Windows-only.

title: BUG: bar/barh plot raises on timedelta64 data containing NaT (GH#39320)
body:
closes #39320

`BarPlot._make_plot` fills missing values with `fillna(0)`. On a `timedelta64` column containing `NaT`, the integer `0` upcasts the column to object (now also a `Pandas4Warning`), after which matplotlib raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'numpy.int64' and 'Timedelta'`. This fills `NaT` in timedelta columns and plots them as their int64 values, which is how matplotlib already drew them. This also avoids matplotlib adding the int `bottom` to `timedelta64` heights, which numpy 2.5 deprecates. The issue's original example (no `NaT`) already works on main.

Stacked line, `area`, `pie`, and `hist` of timedelta values still raise for unrelated reasons (float/timedelta arithmetic); left out of scope, see also GH-17553.

title: CI: add LeakSanitizer job
body:
closes #66140

Adds a `Clang (ASAN/LSAN)` job that runs the same test selection as the existing ASan/UBSan job, but on a CPython built with ASan (and so without pymalloc), with leak detection on. Instead of building CPython, it uses the prebuilt `ghcr.io/nascheme/cpython-asan:3.14` image (pinned by digest), the same one numpy's LSan job uses, and installs the minimal dependencies with pip. Setup and build take ~7 min and the tests ~29 min at `-n auto`, about the same as the existing sanitizer job.

- pytest-xdist kills workers that take more than 10 s to exit, which an ASan build does after a long run, so LSan's exit-time check never runs in them and the job would pass whatever leaked. `ci/lsan_check.py` runs the check at session end in each worker instead. Reports go to files, and a follow-up step fails the job if any exist.
- The only suppression needed is a CPython float from `os.stat()` that isn't freed at exit (`leak:fill_time`). The suite currently has no other leaks.
- UBSan stays in the existing job. Mixing it in here would put both sanitizers' suppressions through the same runtime.

To check that a leak is caught, I removed the `free` of `line_fields` in `tokenizer.cpp`: the job [failed](https://github.com/jbrockmendel/pandas/actions/runs/36368569602) and reported ~197 MB, all from tokenizer allocation sites. With that reverted it [passes](https://github.com/jbrockmendel/pandas/actions/runs/36371154244).

Limitation: LSan only reports memory nothing points to. A missing `Py_DECREF` on an object that stays alive anyway (as in GH-66115 and GH-66033), or on a GC-tracked object, is invisible to it, so this mainly guards raw allocations in the C code.

title: BUG: where/mask mishandled a list `other` for extension dtypes (GH#63842)
body:
closes #63842

`ExtensionArray._where` and `._putmask` index `value[~mask]` directly, which only works if `value` is already an ndarray/ExtensionArray of exactly `len(self)`. Nothing upstream converts a plain list, so a list `other` silently fell back to `object` for `str`/`string[pyarrow]`/`interval` and raised `TypeError: only integer scalar arrays can be converted to a scalar index` for `Int64`/`Float64`/`boolean`/`ArrowDtype` — the reported bug is only the string half of that. `Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and boolean-mask setitem are fixed with it, since they route through the same two methods.

The conversion is done in a new `EABackedBlock._align_listlike_arg`, not in `ExtensionArray`. `_where`/`_putmask` keep their existing contract ("arraylike with the same length as self"), so an EA author still reads the same short method, and `EABackedBlock.where`/`.putmask` are their only callers outside the EAs themselves. Handling it at the block level also reaches `NDArrayBackedExtensionArray` and `SparseArray`, which override `_where` so a fix on the base class never applied to them, and the 2-D datetimelike blocks, where a list reached `np.where` unaligned and silently filled **every** masked position with `other[0]`.

A 2-D block now gets one alignment order: one entry per selected position (putmask only — the analogue of the `np.place` call `putmask_without_repeat` makes for numpy dtypes), then one value per column, then one value per row filling every column. A length that fits none of them raises `ValueError`. The order matters because a consolidated `datetime64[ns]`/`timedelta64[ns]` block holds every column of the frame while `Int64`/`ArrowDtype`/`Categorical`/`datetime64[ns, tz]`/`period` get a block each: before this they gave different answers for the same input, and now they agree.

Non-`Sequence` list-likes — `dict`, `set`, `MultiIndex` — are passed through untouched, so the EA holds them as a scalar (the object-backed dtypes) or rejects them (masked, Arrow, `Categorical`), exactly as before. A tuple is likewise left alone: object dtype holds one as a scalar (GH-37681), and `Index.fillna` admits one.

Note on the conversion: it goes through `com.asarray_tuplesafe` rather than `_from_sequence(dtype=self.dtype)`. `_from_sequence` coerces where we need it to raise — `str` turns `9` into `"9"` and `Categorical` turns an unknown category into `NaN` — and it is the setitem call raising that triggers the block's upcast to `object`.

Base extension tests cover the list shapes, xfailed for `SparseArray` (no item assignment) and `JSONArray` (its `__setitem__` mishandles a boolean mask, which is also the cause of the pre-existing `test_where_series` xfail there).

Not reconciled here: 1-D EA dtypes get one block per column, so they cannot see the frame's column count, and a multi-column EA frame still reads a row-length list per column (`df[key] = [10, 20, 30]`) where the numpy and object spellings raise. That needs the rule moved into `NDFrame._where`, which changes behavior for every dtype and belongs in its own PR. The whatsnew entries are scoped to what actually changed.

title: BUG: tz_localize shift onto the NaT sentinel returned a bogus timestamp (GH#66697)
body:
**Stacked on #66820** — the first two commits here are that PR. Only the last commit (`ff3472d`) is new; I'll rebase this down to a single commit once #66820 lands.

Follow-up to GH-66697, which is closed but left one case behind: a timedelta `nonexistent` shift can land the wall time *itself* exactly on the NaT sentinel. `checked_add` does not flag that — the sum fits in an int64 — so it reaches the transition lookup, which has no meaningful answer for a value sorting below every transition. It resolves to the zone's earliest offset and hands back the sentinel shifted by it, silently:

```python
ts = pd.Timestamp("1933-04-30 02:30").as_unit("ns")
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex([ts, ts])
shift = pd.Timedelta(pd.Timestamp.min._value - 1 - ts._value, "ns")

dti.tz_localize("Pacific/Honolulu", nonexistent=shift).asi8
# array([-9223334150854775808, -9223334150854775808])   <- NaT sentinel + LMT offset
```

On `main` — that is, without #66820 underneath — the same input is worse: `delta_idx` goes to `-1` and indexes `info.deltas` off the front of the array. `tz_localize_to_utc` is `boundscheck(False)`/`wraparound(False)`, so that is a raw read of whatever precedes the buffer: `Pacific/Honolulu` returned a timestamp centuries away while `US/Eastern` raised about the shifted value rather than the one the caller passed, and which of the two you get depends on the heap. #66820 removes the out-of-bounds index; this PR rejects the sentinel, which had no business reaching that lookup either way.

The fix raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, naming the caller's wall time, as soon as the shift lands on the sentinel.

No whatsnew entry: the unreleased v3.1.0 bullet for GH-66697 already describes this behaviour ("... instead of raising `OutOfBoundsDatetime` when the shift leaves the representable range"). A second bullet would read as a separate bug.

The test deliberately uses a two-element index. With one element, `DatetimeIndex.tz_localize` boxes element 0 to compare it against `NaT` and raises there of its own accord, which masks whatever `tz_localize_to_utc` actually returned — a single-element version of this test passes on a tree where the bug is fully live.

title: BUG preserve row alignment in grouped resampling on columns
body:
Fixes #59350.

Grouped resampling on a datetime column can assign values to the wrong time bins when row labels differ from row positions:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "group": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=4, freq="min"),
        "value": [100, 200, 1000, 2000],
    },
    index=[1, 0, 3, 2],
)
df.groupby("group").resample("1min", on="date").agg({"value": "sum"})
```

The values for group a come back as 200 then 100 instead of 100 then 200; group b is similarly reversed. Each group now uses a copied time grouper with its cached state cleared. The sorted branch reverses its positional indexer, while the other branch uses the grouper directly, avoiding label-as-position indexing. Regression coverage includes permuted labels, arbitrary labels, and unsorted dates.

Validation: 336 relevant in-tree tests passed (5 skipped); Ruff checks and formatting pass. CI passed (47 successful checks, 5 skipped). The earlier #59408 PR was closed unmerged and does not cover this multi-group/custom-index reproduction.

title: BUG: MultiIndex setops split a string operand entry into its elements (GH#39699)
body:
Note: this does **not** close GH-39699, which asks for the opposite change — see the last section.

`MultiIndex._convert_can_do_setop` passes a raw list-like operand straight to `MultiIndex.from_tuples`, which accepts any indexable row and so decomposes a string or bytes entry into its elements. When the entry's length matches `nlevels`, the setop treats it as a tuple of level values:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])
mi.intersection(["ac"])              # MultiIndex([('a', 'c')])  -- "ac" is not in mi
mi.union([b"ac"])                    # adds (97, 99)
mi.intersection([("a", "c"), "bd"])  # "bd" matches ('b', 'd')
```

The four setops now raise the existing `TypeError("other must be a MultiIndex or a list of tuples")` for such an operand. Everything else keeps its existing path through `from_tuples`, including `np.void` rows and null entries, which `lib.to_object_array_tuples` deliberately expands to an all-null row.

Two deliberate behavior changes worth a reviewer's attention:

- Splitting a length-`nlevels` label has two outcomes today — it matches spuriously when the characters line up, and returns the right answer by accident when they don't. Both now raise, so e.g. on 2-level columns `cols.difference(["id"])` returned both columns before and now raises. A deprecation cycle isn't really available, since it would mean continuing to return `('a', 'c')` from `mi.intersection(["ac"])` for another release; the `MultiIndex.isin` change in GH-20252 is the local precedent for going straight to raising.
- On a one-level `MultiIndex` a single-character label used to match. Any longer label already raised.

On GH-39699 itself: it asks for `mi.intersection(["some_col"])` to return an empty index, as it did on 1.1.5. That result was the same split — `"some_col"` became an 8-level MultiIndex, which then intersected to empty. Ten existing assertions pin `TypeError` for a raw list of non-tuples, so raising seemed the consistent reading, and I've left the issue open for that separate question.

title: BUG: convert non-native byteorder to native at construction (GH#53234)
body:
closes #53234

Non-native byteorder numeric data (e.g. `>f4` on a little-endian machine) was kept as-is by the Series/DataFrame/Index constructors, so anything reaching a Cython routine raised `ValueError: Big-endian buffer not supported on little-endian compiler` — Index lookups, unique/factorize/value_counts, take/reindex/merge, groupby, window ops, reductions, etc.

This converts to native byteorder at construction (block creation, `Index._ensure_array`, `pd.array` inference), like `DatetimeArray` already does and `Index` did in 1.5. Public functions that accept a raw ndarray (`pd.unique`, `pd.factorize`, `take`) also convert at their Cython boundary. The GH-43042 tests asserting the byteorder is preserved are updated to assert native dtypes with the same values. Also fixes `pd.array` raising `KeyError` on non-native input, and updates the byte-ordering section of the gotchas guide.

title: BUG: support duplicate labels when aligning inputs to binary ufuncs (GH#54416)
body:
closes #54416

Binary ufuncs without an operator equivalent (`np.logical_or`, `np.logaddexp`, ...) aligned their inputs by taking the union of the axes and calling `reindex`, which raises on duplicate labels. They now use `align(join="outer")`, matching what the binary operators (and the ufuncs that dispatch to them, like `np.add`) already do. Ufuncs with more than two pandas inputs keep the old path.

The other behavior in the issue (NaN for non-overlapping columns) is the intended alignment enforced in 2.0 (GH-39239).

title: REGR: fix Series.str.zfill raising ArrowInvalid for negative width with pyarrow-backed strings
body:
- [x] closes #69486
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) — new regression test `test_zfill_nonpositive_width`. Run locally against the pandas nightly wheel 3.1.0.dev0+2043 with pyarrow 25.0.1 and the two changed files applied: `pandas/tests/strings` and `pandas/tests/arrays/string_` give 5612 passed, 0 failed. The new test fails on main (the pyarrow-backed variants raise `ArrowInvalid`) and passes with this change.
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit) — `pre-commit run --files` on both changed files passes every applicable hook locally; pre-commit.ci is green on this PR.
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions — N/A, no new API
- [ ] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature — intentionally omitted: this regression is only on main and hasn't been released yet (same situation as e.g. #61183)

**Root cause.** Since #66339, `ArrowStringArrayMixin._str_zfill` passes `width` straight to `pc.utf8_zfill` for pyarrow >= 21. The Arrow kernel reserves its output buffer based on `width`, so a negative width raises `ArrowInvalid: Negative buffer resize`. `str.zfill` instead returns the string unchanged for any width not larger than the string itself — which is also what the object and python-backed string dtypes do, and what pandas 3.0.x did.

**Fix.** Clamp the width before calling the kernel: `width = max(width, 0)`. `str.zfill` is the identity function for any width <= 0, and `utf8_zfill(width=0)` returns every string unchanged, so the clamped call matches Python semantics exactly. pyarrow's kernel already mirrors `str.zfill` for the remaining edge cases (sign-aware padding for leading `+`/`-`, empty strings, codepoint-based widths, null propagation — all covered by pyarrow's own `test_utf8_zfill`), so no other adjustment is needed. The pyarrow < 21 elementwise path calls `str.zfill` directly and was already correct.

**Tests.** New parametrized `test_zfill_nonpositive_width` (widths -5 / -2 / 0) in `pandas/tests/strings/test_case_justify.py`, executed across all `any_string_dtype` backends and covering signed strings, an empty string, non-ASCII input, and a missing value. On main, the pyarrow-backed variants raise `ArrowInvalid`; with this PR they return the strings unchanged.

**Out of scope.** `str.pad` / `str.center` / `str.ljust` / `str.rjust` raise the same `Negative buffer resize` error for negative widths on pyarrow-backed strings. That behavior predates #66339 (it is present in released 3.0.x), so it is a separate pre-existing inconsistency rather than part of this regression — happy to open a follow-up issue if you'd like it tracked.

title: BUG: avoid segfault in to_json(date_format=iso) on failed allocation …
body:
closes #69461

## Summary

`DataFrame.to_json(date_format="iso")` could segfault when the C
encoder's ISO-datetime conversion (`int64ToIso`, `int64ToIsoDuration`,
`PyDateTimeToIso`) failed — e.g. under a failed memory allocation — and
returned `NULL`. The three callbacks that call these helpers
(`NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback`, `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback`,
`PyDateTimeToIsoCallback`) forwarded that `NULL` to the encoder without
setting `enc->errorMsg`, so `ultrajsonenc.c`'s `JT_UTF8` case (which only
checks `errorMsg`) went on to dereference the `NULL` string.

## Fix

- Each of the three callbacks now sets `errorMsg` when the underlying
  conversion returns `NULL`, so the pending `MemoryError`/`ValueError`
  those helpers already raise propagates instead of being ignored.
- Added a defensive `value == NULL` check in `ultrajsonenc.c`'s
  `JT_UTF8` case as a fallback, so any other `getStringValue` callback
  with the same gap fails safely instead of crashing.

## Testing

Verified against the reporter's own repro (an `LD_PRELOAD` shim that
fails a single targeted `malloc` call): the unpatched build segfaults
at the reported call site; the patched build raises `MemoryError`
cleanly instead. Also ran the existing `pandas/tests/io/json/` suite
locally with no regressions.

I did not add an automated regression test — forcing the specific
allocation to fail is done here via an `LD_PRELOAD` shim outside the
Python process, and I couldn't find a portable way to trigger the same
`NULL` path from pure Python/pytest. Happy to add one if a maintainer
can point me to a pattern used for similar allocation-failure paths.

title: BUG: PeriodIndex partial-string slicing loses anchor on same-resolution labels
body:
Fixes #66571.

Partial-string slicing on a `PeriodIndex` with an anchored freq resolves the string bound one period too early:

```python
pi = pd.period_range("2000Q1", periods=12, freq="Q-FEB")
ser = pd.Series(range(12), index=pi)
ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]
# returns 2000Q4 and 2001Q1 instead of just 2001Q1
```

`_parsed_string_to_bounds` parses the label into a *calendar*-freq `Period` (discarding the anchor month), then converts it back with `asfreq`. When the calendar and anchored quarters don't line up, that round trip spans two periods instead of one. `get_loc` doesn't have this bug because it builds the `Period` directly from `self.freq` for this same case - reused that here.

Ran locally:
```
>>> ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]
2001Q1    4
Freq: Q-FEB, dtype: int64
```

Also ran the full `pandas/tests/indexes/period/` suite (476 tests) plus period-related `indexing`/`truncate` tests (193 tests) - all pass.

title: PERF: Astype dict 63433
body:
All 200 columns get copied before concatenation, which is extremely slow. Instead, implement a shallow copy and replace only the requested columns in place, keeping duplicated column names, metadata and error behaviour.
'''
Benchmark (1000 rows x 200 columns, from the example in the issue):

    case                    main                  this PR
    1 column -> Int64       2.14 ms, 200 blocks   0.17 ms, 4 blocks
    20 columns -> float32   2.53 ms, 200 blocks   0.70 ms, 22 blocks

title: BUG preserve left index dtype in left joins
body:
## Issue

Closes #63371

## Summary?

When two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` first converts them to a common dtype before performing the join. For a `left` join, this can unnecessarily change the dtype of the resulting index.

This PR preserves the dtype of the **left-hand index** for mixed-dtype `left` joins.

The fix applies to one-level indexes across different dtype families, including:

* string
* boolean
* signed and unsigned integers
* nullable integers
* floating-point and nullable floating-point dtypes
* datetime and timezone-aware datetime
* timedelta
* Period
* categorical
* interval
* `RangeIndex`

The original issue was noticed through `Series.str.cat`, where a string index could unexpectedly become an `object` index after alignment. Rather than handling `str.cat` separately, this PR fixes the underlying `Index.join` behavior.

For cases such as incompatible `PeriodIndex`/`DatetimeIndex` joins, the existing behavior is preserved.

## Tests

Added a regression test covering representative one-level index dtypes.

Also updated the existing numeric and `RangeIndex` join tests to reflect the new left-dtype behavior.

## Validation

* Relevant index join tests pass.
* Regression tests for the affected dtypes pass.
* Ruff checks and formatting pass.
* pandas pre-commit checks pass.
* The broader index test suite has one unrelated failure in `TestTZLocalize.test_tz_localize_overflow_tzlocal`.

title: BUG: pandas.array no longer accepts multidimensional data (GH#64280)
body:
pandas.array is documented to be 1-dimensional and to raise ValueError for non-1-D input, but passing an explicit NumPy dtype silently returned a 2-D NumpyExtensionArray. Enforce the documented contract at the pandas.array boundary so the explicit-dtype path raises like the other code paths. Internal NumpyExtensionArray 2-D usage (block operations, GH#38073) goes through __init__ and is unaffected.

`pandas.array()` is supposed to return a 1-D array and raise a `ValueError` when the input contains more than one dimension. However, when an explicit NumPy dtype such as `int64` was provided, passing 2-D data could incorrectly return a 2-D `NumpyExtensionArray` instead of raising the expected error.

The fix adds a dimension check in the explicit-dtype construction path. If the resulting array has more than one dimension, `pandas.array()` now correctly raises the documented `ValueError`.

This change does not affect pandas' internal 2-D use cases, since those arrays are created directly through `NumpyExtensionArray.__init__`, which has been left unchanged.

A regression test was also added to `test_nd_raises` to make sure the 2-D case is properly covered. The change was additionally documented in the `v3.1.0.rst` release notes.

title: CI: open an issue when nightly wheel builds keep failing (GH#55903)
body:
closes #55903

Nightly wheel builds regularly stay red for a week or more without anyone noticing. Since Aug 2025 there have been streaks of 7, 10, 12 and 13 consecutive failed nights, and each failed night also skips the nightly upload to scientific-python-nightly-wheels. GitHub's built-in failure email goes only to whoever last edited the cron line.

This adds a `report_failure` job to `wheels.yml` that runs after scheduled builds:
- On a second consecutive failed night it opens `CI: Nightly wheel builds are failing` (labelled `CI`). A single failed night is ignored, so one-off flakes don't open issues.
- While that issue is open, each further failed night adds a comment.
- Each report links the run and lists the failing jobs plus the pytest `FAILED` test IDs taken from the job logs.
- The next passing night closes the issue.

The job needs only `actions: read` and `issues: write`. It can't be run on a PR, so I ran the script under node with a mocked GitHub client against real logs from the 2026-09-19/20 failures (win_arm64, musllinux_aarch64). zizmor and actionlint are clean.

Adds a monthly (and manually triggerable) workflow that runs [lychee](https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee) over `doc/source/**/*.rst` and the docstrings/comments in `pandas/**/*.py{,x}`, including anchor checks. Why lychee rather than reviving `broken-linkcheck.yml` (GH-55246, disabled in GH-56584, removed in GH-62619): Sphinx `linkcheck` needs a full doc build first, while lychee reads the sources directly and takes about a minute.
