title: BUG: iloc setitem wrote the wrong cells on a Copy-on-Write referenced frame (GH#65446)
body:
Repairs a regression from GH-65864, which is in 3.0.4 and later.

When another object references a `DataFrame`'s values, `BlockManager.setitem` splits the block so only the targeted columns get copied, then re-expresses the caller's column indexer in the new block's coordinates. GH-65864 collapsed any increasing column selection to `slice(None)` and compensated for reordered ones with an array of positions, plus a reshape of the row indexer to `(n, 1)`. Both substitutions change what numpy does: a slice takes the cross product with the row indexer, an array broadcasts against it. So the referenced path could disagree with the unreferenced one in either direction — writing a cross product where the caller asked for an elementwise pairing, or the other way round.

The column indexer now keeps the kind the caller used: an integer stays an integer, a slice stays a slice (reversed if the selection was), `Ellipsis` and `np.newaxis` pass through unchanged, since the new block holds every column in order, and anything else stays an array of positions. The row-indexer reshape goes with it — it was independently wrong, turning an intended broadcast into a cross product whenever `np.ix_` had not already run — and so does the `np.squeeze`, which is only correct for `np.ix_` output; a user-supplied 2-D row key still reaches that spot, and not squeezing it is what makes it match the unreferenced path.

Symptoms fixed, all only when another object holds a reference:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12.0).reshape(4, 3), columns=list("abc"))
ref = df[["a", "b", "c"]]

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::-1] = np.array([100.0, 101.0, 102.0])
# IndexError: shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast
#   together with shapes (2,) (3,)

df.iloc[np.array([1, 0]), range(1, -1, -1)] = 99.0
# silently writes 4 cells; without the reference it writes 2

df.loc[np.array([True, False, True, False]), "c":"a":-1] = 99.0
# IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
```

For the `managers.py` split path the unreferenced path is the oracle: it never enters this code, so referenced-vs-unreferenced is a differential with no shared failure mode. Over 35,728 cases (4 dtypes x 4 frame shapes x 20 row-key spellings x 14 column-key spellings x 7 value shapes, `iloc` and `loc`) `main` diverges in 3,621. The branch's residual divergences are the empty-indexer family, where an early return skips value validation; that predates GH-65864 and is left alone here.

**Depends on GH-68521, which should merge first.** Keeping the column indexer as an array sends 2-D EA blocks (all-`datetime64`/`timedelta64` frames) through the `indexer[::-1]` + `value.T` pair in `EABackedBlock.setitem`, which `slice(None)` had kept them out of. That pair spuriously transposes a 2-D value when both keys are arrays, so on its own this PR would give referenced datetime64 frames the bug unreferenced ones already have (`df.iloc[[2, 0], [0, 2]] = value` writing the transposed cells). GH-68521 fixes it for both. An earlier version of this PR carried its own copy of that fix; it is dropped in favor of GH-68521.

Note for the backport decision: GH-65864 shipped in 3.0.4, so the `IndexError`/`ValueError` families here are live for 3.0.x users. A backport needs GH-68521 as well, for the reason above.

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray silently truncated a value an integer dtype cannot hold (GH#68638)
body:
`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(2, 1.5)` returned `[1, 1, 3]` — the replacement landed, truncated toward zero, with no error and no warning. The numpy-backed Series upcasts to float64 and stores 1.5; the masked `Int64` Series raises `TypeError`. Only the arrow-backed one silently corrupted the value.

`ArrowExtensionArray._validate_setitem_value` boxed the value with `pa.scalar(value, type=pa_type)`, which converts unsafely — `pa.scalar(1.5, type=pa.int64())` is `1`. Because that never raised, the block-level machinery above it never engaged and `putmask_inplace` wrote the truncated value.

This rejects a lossy value in `_validate_setitem_value` with `TypeError`, matching `BaseMaskedArray._validate_setitem_value`. `Series`/`DataFrame` now raise; `Index.fillna`/`Index.where`/`Index.putmask` upcast, since `Index` has no column-dtype contract to protect — both matching the nullable integer dtypes.

The check is a deny-list rather than masked's allow-list on purpose: an allow-list would also turn `arr[0] = "x"` from `ArrowInvalid` into `TypeError`, which is a separate change with its own test fallout.

It runs over list-likes as well as scalars. `pa.array` applies a safe cast to a numpy array but not to a Python list, so `arr[:2] = [9.5, 8.5]` truncated exactly as `arr[0] = 1.5` did while `arr[:2] = np.array([9.5, 8.5])` raised `ArrowInvalid` — the same operation, spelled three ways, silently corrupting in two of them. A non-finite `Decimal` and a `Fraction` fold into the same `TypeError` for the same reason. The scan short-circuits on a container whose own dtype is integer or boolean; other containers pay a few extra passes (measured at 1e6 elements: float64 ndarray 4.8 -> 6.0 ms, object-of-ints 27.1 -> 32.9 ms, int64 ndarray unchanged).

The PyArrow-backed `StringDtype` now accepts a PyArrow *string* scalar in setitem and `fillna` (main rejects it), while still rejecting a non-string PyArrow scalar that pyarrow would cast to its string form. `Series.where` with one previously fell back to `object` and stored a character code: `pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="string[pyarrow]").where([True, False], pa.scalar("xy"))` gave `['a', 121]`.

One behavior change is left unfinished: a 0-d ndarray fill into `Index.where`/`putmask`/`fillna` now raises `ArrowInvalid` after the upcast, where it previously truncated — `_box_pa` cannot box a 0-d ndarray for the widened type. Hoisting the `item_from_zerodim` unwrap out of the integer gate fixes it but regresses `timestamp`/`duration` setitem, so it is left for its own PR.

Adjacent defects found while working on this and deliberately left out: `insert` truncates through `_from_sequence`; `_box_pa_scalar` raises `AttributeError` for a `Timestamp` against a non-matching type; `interpolate`'s linear fast path integer-divides; a dictionary-encoded integer type is not `pa.types.is_integer` and so still truncates.

title: BUG: factorize trusted a pre-encoded pyarrow dictionary
body:
`ArrowExtensionArray.factorize` short-circuited when the input was already `pa.dictionary`-typed and returned the stored dictionary as `uniques`. That dictionary is not a factorization of the values the array currently holds: entries can be unreferenced, they can be duplicated, and a null can live in the dictionary rather than in the indices.

So after an ordinary boolean filter, `groupby` invented a group for a value that was no longer in the frame, while `unique`/`value_counts` on the same column disagreed with it:

```python
enc = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).dictionary_encode()
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": pd.array(enc, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(enc.type)), "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
sub = df[df["v"] > 2]

sub.groupby("k", sort=False)["v"].sum()
# k
# a    4
# b    0   <- "b" appears nowhere in `sub`
# c    3
```

A dictionary holding the same value in two slots additionally split that value across two groups, and a null stored in the dictionary could end up in `uniques`.

The fix re-factorizes in index space — dedupe the stored dictionary, map the indices through it, re-encode, take the uniques back out — so it never materializes the decoded values. Decoding instead silently overflows the 32-bit offsets once the values pass 2 GiB, and the following kernel segfaults. Value types that have no `dictionary_encode` or `take` kernel (nested and view types, `float16`) keep the existing behaviour rather than raising — except under `use_na_sentinel=False` with a null in the indices, where keeping the stored dictionary would leave the null in index space and `factorize` would hand back the `-1` that flag promises not to use; that combination re-raises, as `main` does today.

`uniques` now come out in order of first appearance rather than in the stored dictionary's order, which is what every other dtype does and is visible through `groupby(sort=False)`.

Adjacent defects with the same root cause are left alone deliberately: `_factorize_keys` in `merge`, the `Categorical` constructor, and `unique`/`value_counts`/`mode` all read a stored dictionary the same way, and each needs its own change.

title: BUG: Index.replace raised instead of widening for a value the dtype cannot hold
body:
`Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and `Index.insert` all catch a value the current dtype cannot hold, find a common dtype, and retry on it — `where` was aligned with `putmask` deliberately in GH-39412, on the grounds that an Index has no column-dtype contract to protect the way a DataFrame column does.

`Index.replace` was added later (GH-65099, still unreleased) and delegates straight to `Series.replace`, so it never got the retry:

```python
ci = pd.CategoricalIndex(["a", "b", "c"])

ci.where([True, False, True], "z")   # Index(['a', 'z', 'c'], dtype='str')
ci.replace("a", "z")                 # TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical ...
```

The dtypes affected are Categorical, masked and Sparse — the ones whose `Series.replace` raises `TypeError` for a value it cannot hold. Every numpy-backed dtype already widened, because `Series.replace` upcasts there itself.

Four implementation notes:

- Only `TypeError` is caught, not `ValueError` as in `Index.where`: `replace`'s argument validation raises `ValueError`, and no dtype raises it for a value it cannot hold.
- A replacement whose `to_replace` matches nothing is left out of the common dtype, since `Block.replace` skips those pairs rather than widening for them. Matching goes through `mask_missing`, the predicate `Block.replace` itself matches with — a containment check disagrees with it, notably for an ns-resolution `Timestamp` against object.
- An NA `to_replace` is matched against `hasnans`, and needs no re-check after widening.
- Widening can change how `to_replace` compares (a str, or an ns-resolution `Timestamp`, against datetime categories). When it does, the retry re-raises rather than returning data with the replacement silently dropped. On the regex paths there are no matched literals to re-check, so the retry instead re-raises when it replaced nothing — otherwise a `TypeError` raised for some unrelated reason (`mask_missing` crashes comparing datetime categories against a partial datetime string) would come back as an Index whose only change is its dtype.

Not covered: `Sparse` only widens when the value escapes the Sparse family entirely. `replace(1, 5)` still raises, because the widened dtype is Sparse too and `SparseArray.__setitem__` refuses it just the same (GH-21818) — out of scope here. The behaviour is pinned by a test.

Arrow-backed dtypes are out of scope too, pinned by a test alongside the Sparse one: `pyarrow` raises `ArrowInvalid`, a `ValueError` subclass, so the retry never fires for them. Catching it here would not be enough on its own — arrow's `Series.replace` silently no-ops for a value it cannot hold (`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(1, 1.5)` returns the input unchanged), so that path wants fixing before the Index retry can rely on it.

title: DEPR: reset_index inferring dtype of object index levels (GH#30517)
body:
closes #30517

`set_index` stopped re-inferring object columns in 2.0 (GH-42870), but `reset_index` still infers object-dtype index levels when moving them into columns, so the `set_index`/`reset_index` round trip jreback asked for in the issue is lossy for ints, floats, bools, strings and datetimes alike.

This deprecates that inference: `reset_index` now emits a `Pandas4Warning` when an object-dtype level comes out with a different dtype, and 4.0 will retain object. Calling `infer_objects` on the index (or on each level of a MultiIndex) before `reset_index` keeps the current result and silences the warning.

Nothing inside pandas triggers the warning (the non-slow suite passes with warnings-as-errors). Two tests that incidentally built object-dtype string indexes had the `dtype=object` dropped, since neither is about dtypes.

title: BUG: tz_convert/tz_localize failing or silently wrong with a ZoneInfo built by from_file (GH#64379)
body:
GH-64379 routed every `zoneinfo` timezone through a transition cache that rebuilds the pure-python `ZoneInfo` from `tz.key`. That key only describes the object when it was loaded from the installed tzdata under that key — which is exactly what `ZoneInfo.from_file` need not do. Four ways it goes wrong today:

```python
data = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/US/Eastern", "rb").read()
naive = pd.date_range("2025-06-15", periods=3, freq="h")

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data)))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key="my/custom"))
# ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key my/custom'

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key=5))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

tokyo = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Tokyo", "rb").read()
naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(tokyo), key="US/Eastern"))
# silently uses the installed US/Eastern rules; wrong by 13 hours
```

The last one is the nastiest: it's silent, and it's the realistic case, since pinning a tzdb release via `from_file` under the correct key is a large part of why `from_file` exists. `date_range(..., tz=tz)`, `Timestamp.tz_localize` and the `Series.dt` counterparts all follow the same paths.

## Fix

Gate the fast path on whether `tz.key` is a usable handle at all, rather than assuming it is. `get_zoneinfo_twin` returns a verified pure-python twin or `None`, memoized in a `WeakKeyDictionary` so `from_file` objects don't pin entries; `tz_cache_key`, `is_fixed_offset` and `Localizer.__cinit__` all consult it. When there is no twin, values go down the tzinfo-API path that other zones already use past their last cached transition — no new conversion code.

The test for "was this built by `from_file`" is to ask the object to pickle. The stdlib documents that a `from_file` `ZoneInfo` cannot be pickled, for precisely the reason its key is not a usable handle: the data is not recoverable from the key. So a `__reduce__` that raises `PicklingError` means fall back, and one that succeeds means the object came from the installed tzdata under its key. That is an exact test rather than a heuristic, so `ZoneInfo(key)` and `no_cache(key)` both keep the full fast path and are unaffected.

The cost is that a `from_file` object whose data *does* match the zone its key names cannot be told apart from one whose data does not, so it takes the fallback too — correct, but slower (roughly 30x on a large `tz_localize`; 3ms vs 106ms for 100k values here), and without the fixed-offset shortcut in `DatetimeIndex` set operations, so an empty `intersection` comes back with `freq=None`. Anyone who needs both a non-default tzdb and the fast path can point `zoneinfo.reset_tzpath()` at that release *before the first conversion* and load by key — neither the stdlib’s `ZoneInfo` cache nor pandas’ transition cache is invalidated afterwards.

An earlier revision of this PR tried to close that gap, verifying a candidate twin by probing its transitions and a monthly grid — 0 false rejects across all 598 installed zones, but ~120 lines and a documented residual hole before each zone's first transition. Per review it was dropped in favour of the exact-but-coarser test above; the [commit](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/66828/commits/e8a05a8a8f39c27a6a92c0db4d0685066dff8138) is kept for the record.

`tzdata` stays a Windows-only pixi target. The tests here read a known tzdb file off `zoneinfo.TZPATH`, and fall back to `importorskip("tzdata")` only when the zone is not on `TZPATH` at all — in practice Windows, where `TZPATH` is empty and `tzdata` is already installed. `validate_test_dependencies` cannot see `[target.win.dependencies]`, so it gets an allowlist entry saying why.

The other half of the report this came from — wrong offsets for `Africa/Casablanca`/`Africa/El_Aaiun` in 2088-2099 — is **not** live; GH-65712 and GH-65733 already fixed it. Re-checked against the stdlib across all 598 IANA zones for 2020-2099 (`tz_convert` and `tz_localize`, exact) plus a synthetic reverse-DST zone, so nothing is added for it here.

title: BUG: iloc/loc setitem broadcast a 1-D value down rows on an all-datetimelike frame
body:
`EABackedBlock.setitem` adapted a 2-D EA block's `(ncols, nrows)` storage layout by swapping the two entries of the indexer tuple rather than transposing `values`, since `EA.T` may not be a view (GH-45419). It reoriented only a 2-D ndarray value to match, so a **1-D value was broadcast down rows instead of across the selected columns**:

```python
arr = np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3).astype("i8")
df = pd.DataFrame(arr.view("M8[s]"), columns=list("abc"))

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::2] = np.array([100, 101], dtype="i8").view("M8[s]")
# each value lands in the wrong column, silently:
#   a=101, c=101 in row 0 and a=100, c=100 in row 2
#   expected (and what a float64 frame does): a=100, c=101 in both rows
```

Where the selection could not absorb the misplaced value it raised instead, as `OutOfBoundsDatetime: Incompatible (high-resolution) value` — the `coerce_to_target_dtype(..., raise_on_upcast=True)` fallback reporting a swallowed shape `ValueError` as a resolution problem. The swap was also wrong in other ways: with two list keys or two masks the indexer entries broadcast against each other, so the swap is not a transpose at all, and `Ellipsis`, `np.newaxis`, trailing commas, 2-D keys and non-ndarray values each needed their own handling.

Every 2-D block in pandas is an `NDArrayBackedExtensionBlock` (datetime64, timedelta64, tz-aware, period), whose `.T` is a view. Those now write through `values.T` with the key in frame order, so numpy does the broadcasting and all of the cases above come out the way they do on a NumPy-backed frame. The indexer swap stays as the fallback for a third-party 2-D EA.

When the value genuinely cannot be broadcast, a 2-D block now raises `ValueError: could not broadcast input array from shape ... into shape ...` in frame order, rather than the resolution error.

`test_iloc_setitem_2d_ea_block_matches_numeric` checks this against a NumPy-backed frame over row key × column key × value shape (plus `np.newaxis`, trailing-comma, `range` and 2-D keys) for all four dtypes: 88 of its 144 cases fail on main.

Behavior changes worth calling out, each making an all-datetimelike frame accept or reject what a NumPy-backed frame does:
- an empty value into an empty *row* selection (`df.iloc[[]] = np.array([])`) was a no-op and now raises; into an empty *column* selection it went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to a no-op;
- a column vector into a single column (`df.iloc[mask, 0] = value.reshape(4, 1)`) used to succeed, because the swap's `.T` turned it into a row vector, and now raises; a row vector into a single row (`df.iloc[1] = value.reshape(1, 3)`) went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to writing.

Scope notes, pre-existing and left alone:
- `df.iloc[1, 1] = np.array([x])` still raises where a NumPy-backed frame writes;
- a 1-D block reports a shape failure through the same upcast fallback, as `TypeError: Invalid value ...` or `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. Giving it the new message would change the exception type of `Series` setitem, which wants its own PR.

title: BUG: Timestamp rejected fold with positional date components (GH#52117)
body:
closes #52117

`Timestamp.__new__` validates `fold` before the `if/elif` chain that decides which of the three calling forms is in play. The guard accepted only the keyword-component form or a naive datetime, so the *positional* by-component form — where `ts_input` holds the integer year — fell through to the "possibly unambiguous input" error, whose own advice is to build from components:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
ValueError: Cannot pass fold with possibly unambiguous input: ...
>>> pd.Timestamp(year=2020, month=1, day=1, hour=0, minute=0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')
```

The fix exempts that form too, keyed on both leading arguments being integers rather than on `year` alone, so the guard cannot admit an input the dispatch chain routes to an earlier arm (null-like, `float` and `bool` first arguments all reach `elif` arms above the positional one).

This also removes a limitation GH-31930 documented in the 3.1.0 whatsnew: `datetime.__replace__` reconstructs subclasses through the 8-positional-argument form and passes `fold` when it is nonzero, so `copy.replace()` raised on any `fold=1` timestamp. That clause is deleted and the test pinning it now pins the fixed behavior.

title: BUG: keep left/right index dtype in Index.join on mismatched dtypes (GH#63371)
body:
closes #63371

When the two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` casts both to a common dtype and returned the result in that dtype even for `how="left"`/`"right"`, where every value comes from one side. This follows the thread's consensus to fix left joins generally rather than special-casing `str.cat`, and carries through `align`, `DataFrame.join`, `merge` and `str.cat`. It also removes an asymmetry where `ser1.align(ser2, join="left")` gave a `str` index on one result and `object` on the other. The empty-index path already kept the left dtype.

Behavior change: 14 existing tests asserted the old cast and are updated.

title: BUG: to_csv with quoting wrote float32 values with float64 repr (GH#60699)
body:
closes #60699

With `quoting` other than `QUOTE_MINIMAL`, `get_values_for_csv` casts float columns to object so `csv.writer` sees numbers (and leaves them unquoted under `QUOTE_NONNUMERIC`). That cast turns `float16`/`float32` values into Python floats, which are written with the float64 repr: `8.569999694824219` instead of `8.57`.

This keeps them as numpy scalars instead; `csv.writer` still treats them as numeric and writes their `str()`, matching the default-quoting output. Masked (`Float32`) and pyarrow (`float32[pyarrow]`) arrays are converted to numpy first so they get the same treatment. float64 is unchanged.

title: BUG: zero-pad years before 1000 in default datetime/period formats (GH#58179)
body:
closes #58179

GH-65746 made custom-format `strftime` zero-pad `%Y` for years before 1000, but the default-format paths still printed the year unpadded:

```python
>>> ser = pd.Series(np.array(["0020-01-01", "2020-01-02"], "M8[s]"))
>>> ser.dt.strftime(None).tolist()
['20-01-01', '2020-01-02']     # main; this PR -> ['0020-01-01', '2020-01-02']
>>> ser[0]
Timestamp('20-01-01 00:00:00')  # main; this PR -> Timestamp('0020-01-01 00:00:00')
>>> pd.Period("0020-01-01", freq="D")
Period('20-01-01', 'D')         # main; this PR -> Period('0020-01-01', 'D')
```

This pads the year to 4 digits in the default `DatetimeIndex`/`Series.dt.strftime` paths (which also back `Series`/`DataFrame` reprs), `Timestamp.__repr__`, all `Period` default formats and Period's `%F`. The result now matches `str(Timestamp)`, `Timestamp.isoformat` and numpy (`-020-01-01` for negative years).

The issue proposes an `engine=` keyword to choose between pandas' own formatting and the OS `strftime`. This PR closes it without adding one: with pandas' own paths consistent, the remaining differences are in the OS/Python `strftime` itself and only affect years before 1000. Python 3.14 pads `%Y` on Linux (CPython gh-120713; the 3.12/3.13 backports were reverted).

title: BUG: make Index.get_indexer treat pd.NA as NaN for array/Index targets
body:
- [x] closes #65419

- [ ] I did **not** use AI to develop this pull request.
- [x] I used AI to develop this pull request. I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`, I have reviewed and understood every change, and I have described above how I used it and exactly which tool, model version, and effort setting.

## Summary

`Index.get_indexer` and `Index.drop` treated `pd.NA` inconsistently when matching a NaN label of a string-dtype index:

```python
idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])          # str dtype

idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                       # [0]  (matched NaN)
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))  # [-1]  (bug: did not match)
idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))             # [-1]  (bug: did not match)
idx.drop([pd.NA])                               # worked
idx.drop(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))       # KeyError (bug)
```

`Index.get_loc(pd.NA)` already matches `np.nan`, so the list-target behavior (and scalar lookup) is the intended semantics; the numpy-array and `Index` targets diverged.

Root cause: `Index._maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` normalizes missing values for a `StringDtype` (na_value `np.nan`) target — `target_index.fillna(np.nan)` — but only when the input was a plain list (`not hasattr(target, "dtype")`). Numpy arrays and `Index` objects already carry a `dtype`, so they skipped the normalization and their `pd.NA` kept a different hash than the stored `np.nan`, missing the lookup.

Fix: drop the `not hasattr(target, "dtype")` gate so array/`Index` targets are normalized too, guarded by `target_index.hasnans` (to avoid a no-op copy on NA-free targets) and excluding `MultiIndex` (whose `hasnans`/`isna` raise `NotImplementedError`).

## Verification

- Reproducer from #65419 now returns `[0]` for list, ndarray, `Index`, and `string`-dtype targets, and `drop` works for all target forms.
- Added `test_get_indexer_pd_na_matches_nan` in `pandas/tests/indexes/base_class/test_indexing.py`.
- `pytest pandas/tests/indexes/` → 18087 passed, 244 skipped, 45 xfailed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/indexes/base_class/` → 136 passed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/extension/test_string.py` → 4528 passed, 796 skipped, 20 xfailed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/reshape/` → 2903 passed, 17 skipped, 6 xfailed.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` on touched files → clean.

## Automated contribution disclosure

- Tool: Pi coding agent (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-coding-agent)
- Model: deepseek-v4-pro (via company-newapi)
- Reasoning-effort setting: off

The agent reproduced the inconsistency, traced it to the `not hasattr(target, "dtype")` gate in `_maybe_cast_listlike_indexer`, relaxed the gate with a `hasnans` guard and a `MultiIndex` exclusion, and wrote the regression test. I reviewed the change against the indexing code paths, verified the fix with the reproducer and the indexes/string/reshape test suites, and confirmed no regressions.

title: CLN: use mangle_dupe_names in TextReader header parsing (GH#50371)
body:
closes #50371

GH-66057 moved the python engine's duplicate-header mangling into `pandas.io.common.mangle_dupe_names`, shared with the pyarrow engine. The C engine's `TextReader._get_header` still had its own copy of the same loop. This replaces it with a call to the helper, so all read_csv engines (and `read_html`/`read_excel`, which go through the python engine) use one implementation.

`dedup_names` is left as is. It differs on purpose: it doesn't skip names already in the header, it has no named-before-unnamed ordering, and it doesn't propagate dtypes. That's why the issue's original suggestion of calling it here isn't viable.

Perf: the old loop worked on untyped Python objects, so compiling it gained little. Per header row the Python helper is 1.0–1.26x the compiled loop's time, e.g. ~2 ms on a 100k-column header whose `read_csv` takes ~600 ms.

title: BUG: DataFrame.isetitem and __setitem__ silently corrupted the frame when the value's column count did not match the target
body:
Found by a post-merge audit of GH-65491, which deleted a FIXME reading "refactor, clearly separate broadcasting & zip-like assignment" on the grounds that it was stale. It was not — it marked this defect. No issue was open for it.

`BlockManager.iset` only validated the value's column count under `if lib.is_integer(loc)` — the GH-46544 guard added in GH-66001. With a sequence or slice `loc` nothing checked that `value` had one column per position, so the zip-like branch's `value[placement.indexer]` stored a block narrower than its placement when the value was too narrow, and silently dropped the extras when it was too wide.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.isetitem([0, 1], np.array([7, 8, 9]))   # no exception
df.shape        # (3, 2)
df._mgr.blocks  # (NumpyBlock: slice(0, 2, 1), 1 x 3, dtype: int64,)
repr(df)        # IndexError: index 1 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 1
df.to_numpy()   # (3, 1) -- column "b" silently gone
```

`DataFrame.__setitem__` reaches the same code whenever the key matches several columns (duplicate or `MultiIndex` columns) and the value is one that `_set_item`'s `np.tile` broadcast skips — a timezone-aware `datetime64` or `period` value, or a 2D array:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3]] * 3, columns=["a", "a", "b"])
df["a"] = pd.Series(pd.date_range("2030", periods=3, tz="UTC"))  # same corruption
```

Both reproduce on released 3.0.5 and on 2.3.3; `iset` there has only the row-shape `AssertionError`.

The fix compares against `blklocs`, which is already computed one line above and normalizes int, slice, boolean-mask and integer-array `loc` into a single length, so one check covers every form. The integer-loc guard stays: `_iset_single` returns before the new check, so it is still load-bearing. An empty `loc` writes nothing, so it is exempt and stays the no-op it is on main.

Two things the guard would otherwise have broken are carried here rather than deferred:

- A scalar `value` sanitizes to one column, so `df.isetitem([0, 1], 5)` — which the method's own docstring documents as `value : scalar or arraylike` — would have hit the new check with a message about "1 columns". It now fills every selected position, as the label spelling does, for each `loc` spelling that selects several (list, slice, boolean mask, and the empty forms).
- `_set_item`'s tiling gate was `not isinstance(value.dtype, ExtensionDtype)` where `iset` uses `is_1d_only_ea_dtype`, so exactly two dtype families — tz-aware `datetime64` and `period` — fell between the two and would have gone from silent corruption to `ValueError` while every neighbouring dtype broadcasts. They now broadcast as well; `np.tile` would degrade the EA to object, so that arm uses `reshape`/`repeat`.

The `isetitem` docstring now states the shape rule the new `ValueError` enforces, which was previously only in the error string.

Not fixed here, and filed locally instead: 1d-only EA values still broadcast for a sequence `loc` (`df.isetitem([0, 1], pd.Categorical([...]))`), so `isetitem` semantics still depend on `value.dtype`; a zero-column 2D value slips past the `len(value) > 1` guards in `_iset_single` and `insert` and corrupts the same way, so repairing only the `iset` arm would leave `df[new] = <0-col>` broken; and the `DataFrame`-value branch of `isetitem` counts `len(loc)`, so a boolean-mask loc is counted by the mask's length.

title: DEPR: out-of-bounds scalar setitem into a numpy-nullable integer array (GH#48867)
body:
closes #48867

Redo of GH-68943 (reverted by GH-68971) as a deprecation rather than an immediate raise.

`BaseMaskedArray.__setitem__` now emits a `Pandas4Warning` when numpy stored a scalar altered to fit instead of rejecting it; the 3.x result is unchanged. numpy range-checks a python scalar whatever the key, but a numpy scalar only for a signed dtype under an integer or slice key — so an unsigned dtype with any key, or a signed one with a fancy or boolean key, silently stored the wrong value. That second case covers `where`/`mask`/`replace`/`putmask`, which all arrive with a mask key: `pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int8").where(mask, np.int64(1000))` gives `-24` today. Warning after the store rather than before keeps the paths where numpy raises untouched, without having to encode which key/dtype combinations it checks.

Two notes on the GH-68943 thread. The premise there — that the fillna et al cases "currently actually gave a correct but upcasted result" — holds for the *numpy-backed* dtypes, not the masked ones: every masked path either raises `OverflowError` or stores the value altered, and none upcast. And `Series.fillna` is not covered by this PR, on main or on the branch — it raises `OverflowError` from `scalar_fillna_inplace` before reaching `__setitem__`. Since numpy-backed `where` does upcast, the consistent 4.0 endpoint for masked may be to upcast rather than to raise; worth settling before enforcement.

`shift(fill_value=)` and the float-overflow arm are left alone, as in GH-68943.

title: BUG: loc/iloc setitem raised for a 2D value in a single object cell
body:
Follow-up to a post-merge review comment on GH-66702, where @jorisvandenbossche asked why a 2D value set into a single `object` cell is a shape mismatch rather than simply stored.

It shouldn't be. The answer depended on block layout:

```python
value = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# more than one dtype -> split path
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": [0, 0]})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value
# ValueError: Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an ndarray

# single block -> stored
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": np.zeros(2, dtype=object)})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value  # df.iloc[0, 0] is value
```

Same divergence for a list of `ndarray`/`Series`/`Index`/`ExtensionArray` rows and for a 2-D `ndarray`. Verified identical in 2.3.3, 3.0.6 and `main`, so this is long-standing rather than a regression; GH-64230 and GH-66702 only moved which value kinds reach the raise.

Cause is branch order in `_setitem_with_indexer_split_path`: the `_is_2d_value_for_columns` check runs ahead of the branch that stores nested data in a single cell, so the shape rules for a multi-column selection get applied to a one-cell selection. Single-block frames never take that path, which is why they store.

This moves the single-cell branch above the 2-D check, canonizing the single-block answer. It also hops the "multiple rows in a single column" branch, which is inert here: that branch requires `not is_scalar(pi)`, and `_is_scalar_access` implies `is_scalar(pi)`.

Mostly this is `raise` -> `store`. The exception is a width-1 2D value such as `[[1], [2]]`, which the split path stored flattened (`[1, 2]`) and now stores as given, matching the single-block path.

The test that pinned the old behavior is inverted and re-aimed at the property: it now parametrizes the second column's dtype, which is what decides single- vs multi-block, so the block-layout equivalence is what is under test. With the code change reverted, exactly the 12 multi-block parametrizations fail and the 12 single-block ones pass.

Still divergent after this, left alone deliberately: `df.iloc[0, 0] = some_dataframe` stores the single column as a `Series` on the split path and the whole frame on the single-block path, because the `ABCDataFrame` branch sits above the one moved here.

title: BUG: loc with bool label in object-dtype index or MultiIndex level (GH#50165)
body:
closes #50165

`.loc[False]` raised `KeyError: boolean label can not be used without a boolean index` when `False` was a real label in an object-dtype index or MultiIndex first level (e.g. `[False, 42]`), while `obj[False]`, `obj.loc[(False,), :]` and `obj.xs(False)` already worked. This extends GH-49766, which fixed the bool-dtype-level case.

The check can't simply be removed as the issue suggests: object-dtype lookups match `False` to `0` and `True` to `1` (GH-62888), so `Index([0, "a"], dtype=object).loc[False]` would silently return the `0` row, undoing GH-20432. Instead, a bool key on an object-dtype axis is allowed only when the matched labels are actually bools. An index holding both `0` and `False` still raises, since returning just the `False` row depends on GH-62888.

title: PERF: read_csv parallel reads with index_col
body:
Parallel `read_csv` (GH-64347) used to take the serial path whenever `index_col` was set. The chunk workers now parse the index columns as ordinary columns. After the gather, the index is built by the same `_make_index` a serial read uses, on a reader constructed from the caller's kwargs, so `dtype`/`converters`/`na_values` keyed by the index name behave as they do serially. Invalid `index_col`, repeated positions, tuple names, and implicit-index files still fall back to serial.

Benchmark on a 120 MB `df.to_csv()` file (2M rows, 4 columns plus a string index) read with `index_col=0`, 6 threads, M-series mac: 140 ms → ~30 ms. Reads without `index_col` are unchanged. The tradeoff: an `index_col` read whose chunks disagree on dtype now pays for the abandoned parallel attempt before the serial re-read (~+20% on that file), as non-index reads already do.

title: PERF: avoid copy in MultiIndex .loc with trailing null slices (GH#52714)
body:
closes #52714

`df.loc[(slice(t0, t), slice(None)), :]` went through `MultiIndex.get_locs`, which turned the level-0 slice into a full-length boolean mask, then an intp array, and `.iloc` copied every column with `take`. `df.loc[t0:t]` returns a view of the same rows. On the issue's example (34.7M rows), 12 such slices took 12.7s and peak RSS grew by 3.6 GB. Now each slice takes about 1 ms and does not copy.

A private `MultiIndex._get_locs` returns the level's slice as is when no mask has been built yet and every later key is `slice(None)`. The nested-tuple `.loc` path uses it. Public `get_locs` still returns an ndarray. The existing asv `MultiIndexing.time_loc_slice_plus_null_slice` covers this case.

title: BUG: Index.difference treating parsable strings as datetimelike members (GH#58971)
body:
closes #58971

`Index._difference` resolves membership with `other.get_indexer_for(self)`, and `get_indexer` begins by running the target through `other._maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` — the same label parsing `.loc` and `get_loc` use. For a `DatetimeIndex`/`TimedeltaIndex`/`PeriodIndex` `other`, that turns `"2022-02"` into `Period("2022-02")`, so the string counts as a member. Because the cast is applied to one operand only, the answer depends on which side is `self`: `index2.difference(index1)` came back empty. GH-55108 flipped the lookup direction for perf, which moved which direction shows it rather than introducing it.

Aligning the dtypes before the lookup, as `union` and `intersection` already do, puts that cast out of reach. Membership is then decided by equality, matching `union`, `intersection`, `symmetric_difference` and `isin` — all of which already treat `"2022-02"` and `Period("2022-02")` as distinct, as does `==` on the scalars. `test_float64_index_difference` (GH-35217) pins the same reading, symmetrically, for the float-vs-string version of this case.

The alignment runs only when `other` is a `DatetimeIndex`, `TimedeltaIndex`, `PeriodIndex` or `IntervalIndex`, the types whose `get_indexer` parses or contains labels, so other mixed-dtype calls keep main's path and cost. The same gap existed for `IntervalIndex`, where a scalar contained in an interval counted as a member; that is fixed too. `datetime.date` objects against a `DatetimeIndex` are left on main's path, so they keep matching (with the GH-62158 deprecation warning) until that deprecation is enforced.

Note this makes `index2.difference(index1)` return `["2022-02", "2022-03"]` rather than making `index1.difference(index2)` drop the two periods, so it is the opposite of what the issue asks for and of the stale GH-59148. The dtype comparison is the only added work on the same-dtype path, so GH-55108's speedup is unaffected.

title: PERF: use PyArrow group_by for min/max on Arrow date, time and binary columns
body:
xref #66626

`GroupBy.min`/`max` on Arrow date32/date64, time32/time64, binary/large_binary/fixed_size_binary and null columns had no Cython path, so they fell back to a per-group Python loop (`_agg_py_fallback`). This routes them through PyArrow's native `group_by`, like decimal and string columns already are.

The native path also fixes what the fallback got wrong:
- `min_count` was ignored
- a result that was all NA came back as `null[pyarrow]` instead of the column's dtype
- `large_binary` and `fixed_size_binary` results were demoted to `binary`

`min_count` is now applied with `_if_else` instead of a bare `pc.if_else`. Before PyArrow 24, `pc.if_else` misreads the chunks of a string/binary aggregate, which PyArrow splits once there are more than 32,768 groups (GH#64320, apache/arrow#49410). This also fixes the same corruption for Arrow-backed string columns, which already took this path.

Types without an Arrow `hash_min_max` kernel (decimal32/64, string_view, binary_view, month_day_nano_interval, dictionary, nested types) are unchanged. The ASV benchmark `GroupByAggregateArrowDtypes` gains date32, time64[us] and binary.

Timings, `ser.groupby(keys).min()`, 10% nulls (Apple M1, pyarrow 25.0.0):

| dtype | 200k rows / 1k groups | 1M rows / 100k groups |
|---|---|---|
| date32 | 19.3 → 2.4 ms (8.0x) | 1593 → 22.5 ms (71x) |
| time64[us] | 19.9 → 2.4 ms (8.4x) | 1629 → 22.3 ms (73x) |
| binary | 21.4 → 3.8 ms (5.7x) | 1568 → 40.2 ms (39x) |
| null | 16.9 → 2.0 ms (8.6x) | 1472 → 19.4 ms (76x) |

title: BUG: read_csv names the wrong value when a numeric dtype cast fails (GH#59299)
body:

title: BUG: ops with an iterator raised TypeError instead of treating it as a scalar (GH#31646)
body:
closes #31646

Comparison and arithmetic between a pandas object and an iterator — a generator, `iter([...])`, `map`, `filter`, `reversed` — raised `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` (or `len() of unsized object`), because the op sites gated on `is_list_like(other)` or `lib.is_scalar(other)` and then took a length. NumPy arrays and NumPy-dtype Series already treat an iterator as a scalar.

Two helpers in `pandas/core/ops/common.py` replace those gates across the array and frame op sites:

- `is_listlike_for_op(other)` = `is_list_like(other) and not is_iterator(other)`, replacing `is_list_like`.
- `is_scalar_for_op(other)` = `is_scalar(other) or is_iterator(other) or not (is_list_like(other) or hasattr(other, "__len__") or has_castable_attr(other))`, replacing `lib.is_scalar`. Deliberately not the negation of the first: a sized sequence with `__getitem__` but no `__iter__`, and an operand carrying only `__array__` or `__array_interface__`, are not `is_list_like`, yet NumPy coerces them, so they have to stay element-wise.

Only iterators change. A list-like with no length that can be read more than once — an `Iterable` that is not an `Iterator` — stays on GH-62423's deprecation path and keeps its `Pandas4Warning`.

Iterators become scalar-like now rather than after a deprecation cycle, because the current behavior is a crash rather than a result worth preserving — and the merged GH-62423 deprecation already says non-standard list-likes become scalar-like in 4.0. Two of the three user-visible changes replaced a wrong answer rather than a crash: a `Sparse` dtype and an `ExtensionScalarOpsMixin`-based array consumed a length-matching iterator and computed elementwise, and `ArrowDtype` arithmetic looped forever on an endless one (`ser + itertools.count()`).

Two smaller fixes ride along, since they are the same gate being too narrow to serve as a `len()` guard. An object that is neither list-like nor a recognized scalar now operates as a scalar against a `Sparse` dtype, instead of raising `ValueError` about mismatched lengths, and raises `TypeError` from `&`/`|`/`^` instead of a bare `AssertionError`.

`has_castable_attr` gains `__array_interface__` and `__array_struct__`, which `np.asarray` honors and the widened `is_scalar_for_op` would otherwise misclassify as scalars. That also narrows GH-62423 by the same amount: an operand exposing only one of those warned before and no longer does, so it stays element-wise in 4.0 rather than becoming scalar-like.

GH-31646 is labelled *Needs Discussion*, and the objection recorded there is to returning a boolean array when the lengths do not match. Merged GH-62423 settles that direction for every non-standard list-like, so this PR follows it rather than reopening it.

Related, not addressed here: GH-62423 (the deprecation this follows), and `where`/`mask`/`__setitem__`, which have the same shape but want the opposite resolution, since `pd.Series(gen)` materializes.

title: BUG: DataFrame axis=1 reductions accumulated in each block's own dtype (GH#51474)
body:
Repairs a silent-wrong-answer defect in the block-wise `axis=1` reduction fast path added by GH-65105 (for GH-51474). That PR is unreleased, so the wrong answers never reached users and there is no *Bug fixes* whatsnew entry.

`DataFrame._reduce_axis1` reduced each block in that block's **own** dtype and combined the per-block partials with a numpy ufunc, where the transpose path it replaced reduced in the common dtype of all blocks. On current `main`:

| frame | `axis=1` | `df.T` (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| int64 + float `sum` | `-9.22e18` | `9.22e18` |
| uint64 + float `sum` | `0.5` | `1.84e19` |
| int64 + uint8 `sum` | `4.6e18` (float64) | `4611686018427387906` (int64) |
| float32 + float `sum` | `inf` | `6.0e38` |
| bool + complex64 `mean` | `1.0` | `1+1j` |

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [2**62], "b": [2**62], "c": [0.5]})
df.sum(axis=1)  # -9.223372036854776e+18
df.T.sum()      #  9.223372036854776e+18
```

Compute one cross-block accumulation dtype with `np.result_type` and `astype` each block to it before reducing. For `mean` the accumulator mirrors `nanmean`: float and complex accumulate in their own dtype and widen only at the division, everything else accumulates in float64. `mean` also stops unconditionally casting the combined result to float64, which is what discarded the imaginary part.

Two places then widen the combined result before writing a missing value into it — the `mean` division and the `min_count` null-out. Both now go through one helper that reproduces what `nanops` produces there (float64 for an integer or bool result, complex128 for complex64), and the `min_count` row count is gated on `skipna` so it matches the mask `_maybe_get_mask` actually builds. Without that gate a `complex64` frame reduced with `min_count` and `skipna=False` came back as `complex128` where `df.T` gives `complex64`.

`find_common_type` cannot serve as the accumulation dtype here: it returns `object` as soon as a bool block is present, which would switch the fix off for exactly the bool+numeric frames that reach this path.

There **is** an *Other API changes* entry, for a behavior change GH-65105 itself introduced and did not document: these reductions on a bool + NumPy-numeric mix no longer reduce through `object`, so an integer `sum` or `prod` can overflow and a float result can lose precision where Python's arbitrary-precision arithmetic was exact, and `min`/`max` on a bool + complex mix return a complex result where they previously raised `TypeError`.

Verified against the transpose oracle, the `axis=0` result on the transposed frame, and the single-block frame `df.astype(np.result_type(*dtypes))`, over roughly 260k dtype × block-layout × method × `skipna` × `min_count` cells, with no value or dtype divergence introduced against `main`. Each of the five families above fails if the fix is reverted, and 18 of the 20 new test cells fail on `main`. The residual divergences are two pre-existing families: `min`/`max` still combine per-block partials and so can land on a different dtype than the transpose, and bool-mixed pairs where the transpose itself gives `object`.

title: BUG: read_json(orient="table") could not read back non-string labels (GH#19129)
body:
closes #19129

The issue title asks for a `ValueError`, but on current main the symptom is worse than the 2018 report: an ordinary frame with default `RangeIndex` columns round-trips through `orient="table"` to all-NaN with no error at all.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1.5, 2.5], [3.5, 4.5]])
pd.read_json(StringIO(df.to_json(orient="table")), orient="table")
#     0   1
# 0 NaN NaN
# 1 NaN NaN
```

An int-dtype frame instead raises `IntCastingNaNError` (`Error while type casting for column '0'`), as does a non-string index name; a `MultiIndex` with a non-string level name raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'startswith'` on the *write* side.

The schema field `name` is JSON-serialized from the label, so an int label stays the JSON number `5`, while the record keys in `"data"` are `str(label)` (`"5"`). `parse_table_schema` looked the data up by the schema name and matched nothing.

So this makes the labels round-trip rather than rejecting them. Matching is done on the field name's string form, with the original labels restored at the end.

The fast parser perturbs `0.3` into `0.30000000000000004`, which would otherwise make the match fail for a perfectly ordinary frame. A key that parses back to the same double as the perturbed field name spells that label exactly, so `float()` on the key recovers it. The two are not always the same text — `1e16` is written `10000000000000000.0` in the schema and `1e+16` as the key — so the match is on the parsed value, not the spelling. Labels that no key recovers, including every label when `"data"` has no keys at all, fall back to decoding the document a second time at full precision; worth avoiding, since that decode costs a transient roughly 10x the payload size.

A `"data"` payload of arrays rather than objects has no keys at all, so those labels are used as written. Where `"data"` holds objects, two cases raise `ValueError` instead of reading as NaN: two distinct labels that share a string form (`5` and `"5"`), and a label no key matches when some key matches no field — that orphan key is the evidence the label was spelled differently. Without one the column reads as all-missing, which is what a string label already does.

Two write-side fixes come along because the round-trip needs them: `set_default_names` is guarded against a non-string `MultiIndex` level name, and a falsy `Series` name (`0`, `False`, `""`) is no longer replaced by the `"values"` placeholder — only a `None` name is a missing name.

Not addressed here, and left for a follow-up on the write side: `None`, tuple, and duplicate labels still emit a schema `name` that disagrees with the data keys. The full remedy is to derive the schema `name` from the same stringification the C writer uses for object keys, which is a larger change to `build_table_schema` than this needs. GH-25488 proposed switching the data payload to `orient="values"` arrays — correct diagnosis, too invasive.

title: BUG: partial string indexing that matches no entries raises KeyError (GH#57596)
body:
closes #57596

`DatetimeIndexOpsMixin._partial_date_slice` raised `KeyError` when a partial-string key fell outside the index's range, but returned an empty selection when it fell inside and matched nothing. Callers that need presence semantics — `Index.__contains__`, `.at`, and `.loc`-setitem's missing-key path — read that as a match of length zero, so the assignment in the issue silently set nothing. It now raises `KeyError` whenever the selection is empty, which also makes an in-range miss consistent with the out-of-range case that already raised, and with a `MultiIndex` datetime level, which already raised.

The two `# we are out of range` pre-checks are removed as part of this: they fire only when both bounds lie past the extreme element of a sorted index, which is exactly when the new check raises anyway.

This is a behavior change for getitem — `ser["2024-05"]` where May is absent but in range now raises instead of returning an empty Series — so it has a notable-bug-fix whatsnew entry. Nothing in the test suite asserted the old behavior.

This reverses my earlier suggestion on the issue to catch this outside `get_loc`. On main, `get_loc` already raises `KeyError` for a partial string whose window lies entirely outside the index's range; it only returns an empty result when the window falls in a gap inside the range. This PR makes the in-range case agree with the out-of-range one. Fixing it in the `.loc` setitem path alone would leave `key in dti` returning `True` and `ser[key]` returning an empty Series for a key that `.loc` then treats as absent.

title: BUG: astype/construction from float to datetime64 is an unchecked narrowing
body:
A ``float`` outside the ``int64`` domain cast to ``M8``/``m8`` was silently converted. Positive overflow saturated to ``INT64_MAX`` and read back as a real-looking timestamp; negative overflow landed on ``INT64_MIN``, which *is* the ``NaT`` sentinel, so ``-inf`` became missing data. The only signal was a numpy ``RuntimeWarning``, which pandas does not promote.

```python
pd.Series([np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.Series([-np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]   # NaT
pd.Series([1e30]).astype("m8[s]")[0]       # Timedelta('106751991167300 days 15:30:07')
pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.inf]))[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.to_datetime(np.array([np.inf]))[0]      # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
```

The timedelta64 family was already guarded by ``cast_from_unit_vectorized``'s ``_raise_if_outside_int64``; datetime64 was the unguarded member, so ``.astype`` disagreed with ``dtype=``, and ``DatetimeIndex`` disagreed with ``TimedeltaIndex`` on the same input. This adds the same check to the two sites that lacked it — ``_astype_nansafe``'s fall-through cast and ``maybe_convert_dtype`` — reusing the message the timedelta peer already emits so the two agree.

``errors="coerce"`` is preserved: ``to_datetime`` blanks just the out-of-range entries rather than letting the raise escape, matching what ``to_timedelta`` already does (GH-66823).

`is_float_dtype` is true for ``Float64``, so ``maybe_convert_dtype`` fired for masked input while ``_astype_nansafe`` — which only sees ndarrays — did not, leaving ``DatetimeIndex(masked)`` raising and ``.astype``/``dtype=`` on the same array silently wrong. `BaseMaskedArray.astype` gets the guard too, so the three spellings agree. The pyarrow-backed and ``Sparse`` float spellings were silently wrong on all three and are covered by the same two sites.

The guard is skipped for a multiplier dtype such as ``M8[10s]``, which pandas rejects outright whatever the values; without that gate an out-of-range float turned a ``ValueError`` about the dtype into an ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` naming a unit the user never asked for. One known consequence remains: ``Index([inf]).astype("M8[D]")`` now raises ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` where it raised ``TypeError`` before. Deferring to that ``TypeError`` is not reachable without dropping the guard for ``Series.astype("M8[D]")``, which on main silently turns ``-inf`` into ``NaT``; both arms raise either way, so this narrows the data-dependent-exception problem rather than removing it.

In-range values are untouched, including the deliberate ``float(iNaT)`` → ``NaT`` mapping and ``NaN`` → ``NaT``. Not covered here, and tracked locally instead: ``uint64``, ``complex`` and ``Categorical`` sources, each of which needs a different predicate or a separate API decision.

title: BUG: replace silently discards a compiled regex on ArrowDtype strings
body:
`Series.replace`/`DataFrame.replace` silently discarded a compiled `re.Pattern` on arrow-backed string dtypes:

```python
pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())).replace(re.compile("^a"), "z")
# ['a', 'b']   <- discarded; object, str, string[python] and string[pyarrow] all substitute
```

`Block._replace_regex` gated compiled patterns on a literal allowlist, `_regex_target_dtype(self.dtype) not in [object, "string"]`. `ArrowDtype(pa.string())` matches neither, so the pattern never reached `replace_regex`. The string spelling of the same pattern was unaffected — `is_re("^a")` is False, so it never hit the guard.

The allowlist is now `is_string_dtype(target) and target.kind != "S"`. The `kind != "S"` half keeps numpy bytes out, since `is_string_dtype` counts them and a regex can never match bytes (without it a `|S2` Series silently upcast to `object` on what is still a no-op). The predicate is still applied to `_regex_target_dtype`, which resolves a `Categorical` to its categories' dtype (GH-68928), so a `Categorical` of arrow strings stops being a silent no-op too.

Widening the gate is not enough on its own: the object-upcast escape hatch on the next lines asks `can_hold_element`, which returns `True` for every `ArrowDtype` (`pandas/core/dtypes/cast.py`, under the comment "This is technically incorrect"), so an unholdable replacement never triggered the upcast. That is already visible on the released string spelling — `replace("^a", 1, regex=True)` raises `ArrowInvalid` and `replace(regex={"^a": 1})` silently stores `"1"`, where every other string dtype upcasts to `object` — and the compiled spelling would join them once the gate admits it. For an arrow string block the decision is now made directly: a `str`, a regex (left to raise on write, as `StringDtype` does), or a scalar NA fits, and anything else upcasts. That branch is gated on the same string predicate, so a non-string arrow column keeps its dtype through a frame-wide sweep like `df.replace(r"^\s*$", 0, regex=True)`.

Not covered here, each a separate defect with its own review surface: dictionary-encoded arrow strings, which `is_string_dtype` rejects, and `pa.string_view()`, where the direct path discards silently just as `string` did while the `regex=` dict path raises `NotImplementedError` from `ArrowDtype.type`, so admitting it to `is_string_dtype` would not be enough. Also, non-regex `replace` makes the same always-fits check and still raises for a value that doesn't fit (`ser.replace("a", 1)`), so the regex and non-regex spellings disagree until that is fixed separately.

title: PERF: out-of-band pickling of a sliced DataFrame (GH#55781)
body:
closes #55781

numpy serializes an ndarray out of band (PEP 574) only when it is C- or F-contiguous, so a sliced `DataFrame` — whose block values are a strided view of the parent — had its data copied into the pickle stream rather than shared with the consumer. `Block.__reduce_ex__` now makes such a block contiguous when the protocol can actually use a buffer.

The gate is `protocol >= 5` on a non-contiguous, non-object ndarray. Below protocol 5 the copy is waste: numpy copies again via `tobytes` and peak memory doubles. Object dtype numpy refuses out of band whatever the layout, as it does `datetime64`/`timedelta64` — which is why extending this to the EA-backed blocks would buy nothing. At protocol 5 peak memory is unchanged, since main already paid a `tobytes` copy on the same block, while an out-of-band consumer goes from 0 buffers to 1.

Two things worth flagging for review. The issue's own reproducer no longer shows the bug — block layout has changed since it was filed, so a column slice is already contiguous; the surviving case is the row slice, which is also the one that matters to the frameworks in the report, since they partition by rows. And the win is confined to out-of-band consumers: `pickle.dumps` defaults to protocol 4, and `to_pickle` passes no `buffer_callback`, so neither changes.

Only block values are covered. A step-sliced frame's `Index` and a `Series`' values reach the pickler by other routes and still go in band.

title: DEPR: pinning group key to name attribute in groupby UDFs
body:
closes #41090
closes #25457
closes #45894

## Summary
- Deprecate pinning the group key to the ``name`` attribute of the group passed to a user-defined function in groupby ``apply``, ``transform``, and ``filter``, and in the ``Resampler`` equivalents (GH-41090). The warning's migration recipe is given per method: ``pd.concat({key: func(group) for key, group in gb})`` reproduces ``apply``, while ``transform`` and ``filter`` return an object indexed like the original and need their own recombination
- The key is still pinned exactly as before (no behavior change), but flagged via a private ``NDFrame._groupby_pinned_name`` attribute; ``Series.name`` and ``DataFrame.__getattr__`` emit a ``Pandas4Warning`` when user code reads the pinned name. Internal reads (e.g. result-name propagation in ops) are exempted by classifying the single frame that did the read, so UDFs that never touch ``.name`` see no warning
- Compared to a call-without-name-then-retry approach: the UDF runs exactly once per group, Series groups keep returning the group key (rather than silently returning the column name), and exceptions from UDFs surface unchanged
- The key is no longer written into the group's instance ``__dict__``, so two paths need explicit handling to keep the pre-deprecation behavior. ``NDFrame.__setattr__`` short-circuits ``group.name = value`` so that it sets an attribute and unpins, rather than falling through to assigning a *column* named ``"name"``. And ``_pin_deprecated_group_name`` drops a ``name`` that ``__finalize__`` propagated from a subclass's ``_metadata``, which would otherwise shadow ``__getattr__`` and hide the key entirely
- Groupby plotting (``.plot`` accessor, ``hist``) goes through ``_python_apply_plot``, which labels each Series group with its key explicitly, so enforcement can delete the deprecation machinery without touching plotting. That helper has since landed on ``main`` separately; this branch now just rebases onto it
- At enforcement, ``name`` inside a UDF is never the group key: a ``"name"`` column is no longer shadowed (GH-25457), and ``apply``/``transform``/``agg`` stop disagreeing about what ``name`` is (GH-45894, resolved in the opposite direction from the reporter's proposal)
- Removed the docstring notes advertising the ``name`` attribute from ``GroupBy.apply``, ``SeriesGroupBy.apply``, both ``transform`` docstrings, and ``DataFrameGroupBy.filter``

**Known limitation:** the warning fires only on direct ``.name`` access. A UDF that hands the group to pandas code that consumes the name internally (e.g. ``x.to_frame()`` naming the column after the key) does not warn now and will change behavior at enforcement. Exempting only the readers that use ``self._name`` explicitly was tried and rejected: instrumenting the hook across the groupby, resample and apply suites turns up 13 distinct internal readers, so that variant would warn on ``group + 1`` and ``group.value_counts()``.

**Cost:** ``Series.name`` reads go from ~37.5ns to ~62.8ns locally, worth ~4% on ``small + small``. The guard is one attribute load in a property whose body is otherwise a single load, so the cost is inherent to intercepting reads; spelling it as an instance-``__dict__`` membership test measured no better.

The exemption check itself is a single-frame lookup rather than ``find_stack_level``: the question is only whether the frame that read ``.name`` is pandas' own code, and ``find_stack_level`` answers it by walking the whole pandas prefix — 10+ frames inside a groupby transform — on a path taken about five times per group.

## Test plan
- [x] Full groupby, resample, and plotting suites pass (warnings escalate to errors in the test suite, so this also verifies no spurious warnings)
- [x] Plotting suite additionally passes with pinning disabled entirely (enforcement simulation)
- [x] New tests: Series group ``.name`` returns the group key with a warning; UDFs not touching ``.name`` don't warn; name set inside a UDF unpins; ``SeriesGroupBy.plot(legend=True)`` legend labels are group keys; ``DataFrameGroupBy.filter`` and the three ``Resampler`` entry points warn; setting ``group.name`` does not clobber a ``"name"`` column; a subclass with ``name`` in ``_metadata`` still sees the key
- [x] mypy, pyright, pre-commit clean

title: TYP: remove mode from BaseBuffer protocol (GH#60660)
body:
closes #60660

`BaseBuffer` required a `mode` property, so objects like `io.IOBase` and botocore's `StreamingBody` failed to type-check as `ReadBuffer`/`ReadCsvBuffer`. Removing it also makes `GzipFile` (whose `mode` is an `int` in typeshed) satisfy the protocol, so an unused `type: ignore` is dropped.

This loosens the protocol, so nothing changes at runtime. pandas-stubs has the same `mode` property and will need a matching change for most type-checker users.

```python
df.sort_index(axis=1, level="B", key=lambda x: np.argsort(index_natsorted(x)))
# KeyError: 'Level B not found'
```

`level=1` works, as does a key that returns a named `Index`. `_ensure_key_mapped_multiindex` applies the key to each level and rebuilds the `MultiIndex` with `from_arrays(mapped)`, which takes the names from the mapped arrays. A key that returns an ndarray gives an unnamed level, so `sortlevel("B")` can't find it.

As @rhshadrach suggested in the issue, the name is now set internally rather than requiring the key to return a named `Index`: the rebuilt `MultiIndex` gets `names=index.names`. `ensure_key_mapped` already wraps the key's result in an `Index`, so no other change is needed. This only affects `MultiIndex`, since `level` is a no-op on a flat index.

The test sorts by level name with a key returning an ndarray, on both axes, and fails on main. The sort tests in `tests/frame/methods`, `tests/series/methods`, `tests/indexes/multi/test_sorting.py`, `tests/test_sorting.py` and `tests/indexes/test_base.py` pass (2078 passed).

`DataFrame.plot` accepts a `color` argument, but the argument is missing from
its API documentation. This adds the parameter to the canonical plotting
accessor docstring and documents the supported string, array-like, and
column-to-color dictionary forms.

Verification:

- Compiled `pandas/plotting/_core.py`.
- Rendered the `pandas.DataFrame.plot` API page with warnings treated as errors.
- Confirmed that `color` appears between `colormap` and `colorbar` with the
  expected type and description.

Oh My Pi with OpenAI Codex `openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol` was used to inspect the
repository guidance, locate the canonical docstring, draft the documentation
change, and assist with verification. The harness does not expose a separate
reasoning-effort setting. I reviewed and understood the change and remain
responsible for the contribution.

title: CI: Decline /untake if the contributor has an open PR
body:
Written by Claude Opus 5.5.

We've seen cases where contributors `/untake` their existing issues in order to get around the limit (2) of assigned issues. Currently when this happens their PR remains open, allowing them to game the contributing system. This PR addresses this by refusing an `/untake` when there is a linked PR still open. It also includes when there is a PR that was once linked but no longer closes an issue in order to avoid contributors unlinking the PR first.

title: DEPR: cache_dates in read_csv, read_table, read_fwf (GH#68705)
body:
closes #68705

Deprecates the `cache_dates` keyword in `read_csv`, `read_table`, and `read_fwf`. Omitting it keeps the current behavior (caching on) with no warning; passing it explicitly emits a `Pandas4Warning` pointing to `pd.to_datetime(..., cache=...)`.

With the C engine, ISO dates never reach `to_datetime` (they take the char-buffer fastpath), so the keyword only matters for non-ISO / `dayfirst` / index-column parsing. Caching stays on by default since it is a large win on duplicated dates; `cache_dates=False` only helps when the uniqueness sample misjudges a mostly-unique column (~35% in a constructed worst case).

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used to investigate the caching paths, write the patch and tests, and run the test suite; I reviewed the diff.

title: DOC: note unicode case-mapping differences between str dtype storage variants
body:
the migration guide for the new string dtype states "all string-specific methods through the str accessor will work the same", but that sentence is contradicted by the known-differences list in #63105: whether pyarrow is installed changes str accessor results for unicode case mappings

```python
# pandas 3.0.6, same dtype both times
>>> pd.Series(["ß"], dtype="str").str.upper().item()   # pyarrow installed
'ẞ'
>>> pd.Series(["ß"], dtype="str").str.upper().item()   # no pyarrow
'SS'
```

the same family affects related case-mapping characters (e.g. lowercasing "İ" gives "i" with pyarrow storage but "i̇" with python storage) and can change string lengths, which is easy to hit in groupby/join keys or tests that pass on one machine and fail on another

this adds a note right under the "will work the same" example pointing to the tracking issue #63105 so readers know the guarantee has known unicode exceptions

found while cross-checking case-mapping behavior across pandas, polars, pyarrow and duckdb for narwhals docs (narwhals-dev/narwhals#3986)

title: BUG: assert_series_equal check_exact=True no longer forces an array-class check (GH#56132)
body:
…lass check (GH#56132)

With check_exact=True, assert_series_equal routed non-ExtensionArray values through assert_numpy_array_equal, whose assert_class_equal step reported the underlying array *class* as different (e.g. numpy.ma.MaskedArray vs. ndarray) even though the default check_exact=False comparison performs no such check.

Coerce those values to a base ndarray before the comparison so that check_exact governs only how the values are compared, not whether the array class is checked, matching the default path. assert_frame_equal is fixed as well since it delegates the per-column comparison to assert_series_equal.

AI Usage Details: I used Gemini 3.1 Pro strictly to assist with the analysis part of the codebase. I personally wrote, reviewed, and understand every line of the final code and tests. We also ran full test suites to guarantee correctness.

### Background

Fixes #20442. In pandas, `None` is generally treated as a missing value similar to `np.nan`, meaning that equality comparisons against `None` should evaluate to `False`. While `Series([None]) == Series([None])` correctly short-circuits to evaluate to `False`, using the method explicitly like `Series([None]).eq(Series([None]))` incorrectly evaluated to `True`.

### Fix

Modified `pandas/core/series.py` in `_binop` so that comparison operators (`operator.eq`, `operator.ne`, etc.) explicitly route through `ops.comparison_op`. This ensures that `.eq()` and `.ne()` apply the same missing value handling rules as the native `==` and `!=` operators, enforcing the expected consistency for `None`.

### Verification

Added unit and regression testing in `pandas/tests/series/test_arithmetic.py` specifically enforcing parity between `==` and `.eq()` for `None` values.

title: BUG: Fix resampling with CustomBusinessDay/BusinessDay and closed='right'
body:
Resampling with end-of-period offsets like `CustomBusinessDay` ("C") and `BusinessDay` ("B") was not correctly aligned when `closed="right"`.

In `pandas/core/resample.py` line 2701 (inside `_adjust_bin_edges`), the function only checked for specific end-of-period offsets like `"BME"`, `"ME"`, `"W"`, etc., but did not include `"B"` (BusinessDay) or `"C"` (CustomBusinessDay). When `closed="right"`, these offsets also need their bin edges rolled forward to the last moment of the day, otherwise data on the last day overflows into a new/extra bin containing `NaN` at the end and casts integer columns to `float64`.

This PR:
1. Updates `_adjust_bin_edges` to check for `"B"` and `"C"` as end-of-period offsets.
2. Adds a regression unit test `test_resample_custom_business_day` to verify correct binning and dtype preservation for `CustomBusinessDay` resampling.

Closes #65740
